items.title: When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research
items.content: arXiv:2611.25198v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.

items.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
items.content: arXiv:2611.25360v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.

items.title: Whose Risks Count? What 1,901 AI Incidents Reveal About Corporate Disclosures
items.content: arXiv:2611.25841v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI systems can harm people, yet the AI actors that provide or deploy them are rarely obliged to disclose these risks. US securities regulation is an exception. Companies registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) must disclose their material risks, including those of their AI systems, in filings that carry liability for misstatement. Materiality, however, is defined by what a reasonable investor would consider important, so harms to third parties enter disclosure only insofar as they become financial risks for the company. We test whether AI harms do so by matching 9,001 AI incidents to 18,229 SEC filings of 328 AI actors by risk type. Of the 1,901 incidents with filings before and after them, half belong to a risk type that the AI actor never disclosed, and this share varies with the kind of harm. Filings disclose the risk types of 67\% of system failures but only 2\% of social system harms, and AI actors themselves report fewer than 2\% of incidents. Securities disclosure thus records the risks that AI actors face rather than the harms that people subject to AI bear. Public authorities that hold AI actors accountable for such harms could make them financially material. We release DISC, the Disclosure--Incident Securities Corpus, to support this work.

items.title: What the model knows but does not say: monitoring medical LLMs through verbalized thoughts
items.content: arXiv:2611.24994v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Efforts to keep clinical language models safe have concentrated on what enters and leaves the model, but a manipulated model can return an answer that looks entirely ordinary. Here we show that the model's own internal state, rendered in plain language, exposes manipulations the output conceals. Using a natural-language autoencoder, we translate the activations of a multimodal LLM (Gemma-3-27B) into text and let an input-blind judge read this verbalized internal state (the thoughts channel) and the model's answer separately. Across two clinical attack objectives (omitting a pathology, covertly recommending a drug), two input modalities, and two delivery mechanisms, the thoughts channel caught the injection significantly more often than the answer in all eight injected conditions (p<0.05), while both channels held near-zero false-positive rates on clean inputs; the omission result carried over to Llama-3.3-70B. The thoughts channel also registered unsafe clinical requests as harmful while the model was still reading them, before it decided whether to refuse. None of this requires retraining: an off-the-shelf verbalizer and a general-purpose judge are enough.

items.title: Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25226v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.

items.summary: This paper identifies a critical weakness in image watermarking: from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, attackers can forge the watermark onto arbitrary content, falsely attributing harmful images or making authentic photos look AI-generated. The authors argue watermarking schemes should not only reject forgeries but also report them, leaving forensic evidence of the attempt, and propose a scheme meeting accuracy, robustness, undetectability, and forgery-evidence requirements.

items.title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery in PHP Web Applications
items.content: arXiv:2611.25412v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain.   We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection. Object-centered chaining knowledge from our empirical study directs searches toward promising vulnerability classes, functional operations, and object accesses. ChainAgent achieves 42.02%--44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct goal-reaching dependency edges as Codex. An additional evaluation of 30 real-world PHP applications identifies 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine of which achieve remote code execution (RCE).

items.title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25719v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.

items.title: Web search in Latin America: language models use less local and diverse news than search engines
items.content: arXiv:2611.25955v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI platforms are becoming a major gateway to news and current events. This shift risks amplifying existing geographical biases that favour narratives from wealthier countries over those from the Global South. This is particularly relevant in Latin America, which accounts for the largest share of AI usage in the Global South. We examine how information about Latin America changes when users shift from conventional search engines to LLM-based search. We construct a dataset of 1,901 current events across nine Latin American countries, craft realistic queries, and submit them to three search engines and four language models. We vary query language and user location to represent local, diaspora, tourist, and foreign user scenarios. Across 49,207 requests and 8,834 unique domains, language models return a less diverse set of news sources than search engines. Across user types, the share of domestic news returned by language models is inconsistent. For local users, while search engines already return only 41.3\% local news, language models return a further 3.6 to 11.6 percentage points less. Taken together, our findings suggest that LLM-based search can reproduce and, in some settings, amplify geographical hierarchies in the reach and visibility of news sources. We release an open dataset to support multilingual and geographically diverse evaluation of LLM-based search, and highlight implications for more equitable information systems design.

items.title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.26617v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

items.title: RouteVerify: Routing Interventions for Step-Level Verification in Mixture-of-Experts Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25780v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Routing states in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps. If changing routing also changes a model's step-level verification judgment, it is tempting to conclude that the judgment follows what routing encodes. We test this inference with RouteVerify, a controlled intervention study that replaces selected internal activations from one solution trace with activations from another, while keeping the evaluated input unchanged. Across nine MoE checkpoints, we compare three intervention interfaces: router logits, MoE outputs, and post-MoE residual states. We vary the layers and token positions at which activations are replaced. We measure changes in a verification margin that quantifies the model's preference for INCORRECT over CORRECT. We also evaluate the same input with activations from correct versus erroneous steps to test whether the resulting judgment depends on the source step's correctness. We report four linked results. First, probes on router logits separate correct from erroneous steps in eight checkpoints (AUROC 0.80-0.88). Second, replacing router logits across all routed layers changes the judgment in all nine checkpoints, and by more than a norm-matched random replacement. Third, this change rarely depends on whether the source step is correct. At one layer, routing from erroneous steps and from correct steps produces indistinguishable margins in all nine checkpoints. Under all-layer routing, their difference is resolved and positive in only one. Fourth, the same difference is positive for local residual replacements in eight of nine checkpoints, so the measure does detect such dependence where it exists. Correctness is therefore readable from routing, and routing replacements move the judgment, but the movement rarely follows correctness.

items.title: Learning to Compare Neural Representations from Parameterized Computation Graphs
items.content: arXiv:2611.26081v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Comparing internal representations across trained models is important for identifying corresponding layers and selecting components for model reuse. Yet, direct comparisons at inference require evaluating candidate models on known reference inputs and collecting their internal activations. In this paper, we study whether internal representation similarity measured across independently trained models can instead be learned to predict in unseen models from their parameterized computations. We introduce a framework that applies a graph metanetwork for mapping each internal site to an embedding derived from its upstream computations while accounting for hidden-coordinate permutation and internal attention-basis transformations. We analyze the structural properties of our estimators and derive conditional guarantees for layer retrieval and stitching candidate selection. Empirically, we find that the learned predictors support relation estimation and low-regret layer retrieval. They also select useful stitching connections while not being trained on stitching outcomes. This opens up a new way to study representation similarity directly from trained neural networks: representational relations learned across a collection of trained models can generalize to new computations, and that the predicted relations can guide candidate selection before direct measurement or adapter fitting for functional evaluations.

Practical utility depends on generalization to very heterogeneous architectures.

items.title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2611.26157v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.
items.author: Doyeob Kim
items.summary: NariQ is a trellis-coded post-training quantization method calibrated on tokens generated by the BF16 model during agent sessions, addressing the mismatch between standard short-context calibration and long-horizon agentic workloads. On Qwen3.8-27B, an existing open model, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight matches BF16 on DeepSWE and Terminal Bench as well as AIME, whereas prior sub-3-bit quantizations solve at most 72% of long-horizon tasks.
items.reasoning: Highly relevant to practical LLM deployment: it identifies and fixes a real, quantified failure mode (quantization degradation specifically on long-horizon agentic benchmarks) with a concrete calibration fix. Single-author work and evaluation on one model family temper the score, but the finding that perplexity-based evaluation masks agentic degradation is broadly important.

items.title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2611.25061v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/

Coupling a generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting module prevents degenerate outputs and improves robustness on out-of-distribution scenes where feedforward networks degrade.
items.reasoning: A conceptually attractive alternative to feedforward 3D reconstruction with strong author credibility (MIT/affiliated researchers including Tenenbaum, Freeman, Sitzmann, Du). The cognitive-science-motivated framing and OOD robustness results make it a notable contribution, though inference-time optimization may limit practicality.

items.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
items.content: arXiv:2611.26569v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.
items.author: Ziqing Yang, Yixin Wu, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
items.summary: The authors introduce EditSafetyBench, a 5,940-pair benchmark evaluating system-level safety of instruction-guided image editing across 11 risk categories and three edit intents, probing both safe and unsafe uploaded images. Evaluations of four systems including Gemini, GPT, and Qwen APIs reveal a systematic text-vision safety gap: safety mechanisms attend to text prompts while largely ignoring risky visual content.
items.reasoning: Timely and important AI safety contribution with a substantial benchmark and a clear, actionable finding about modality-blind safety filtering in deployed commercial systems. Broad relevance to multimodal model safety, though evaluation of a small set of systems.

However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

items.title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.25813v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.

items.title: Learning to Think with Images Faithfully via Adaptive Data Selection
items.content: arXiv:2611.26199v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning. However, our analysis shows that the improved accuracy of TwI models does not guarantee faithful tool use; they frequently invoke tools without actually relying on the zoomed region, undermining the reliability of tool-assisted reasoning. We trace this unfaithful behaviour to the training data: when questions are answerable without zooming, the model can answer correctly while ignoring the returned evidence, and this problem is exacerbated during training as the model becomes better at answering without tools. To keep zooming useful throughout training, we adapt the training data to the model's evolving capability and train on questions where correct zoomed evidence can still help the model answer correctly. This selection is supported by a data synthesis pipeline that localises small objects and constructs verifiable questions about their fine details, and complemented by an adaptiveness reward that favours tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary. The experimental results show that our method substantially improves reasoning faithfulness and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual search benchmarks (+11.6% on V*, +7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and +9.4% on HR-Bench 8K). On multimodal hallucination benchmarks, our model also outperforms the compared TwI baselines. These results suggest that improving TwI faithfulness does not sacrifice accuracy and that both can be learnt from the right training data without directly supervising the reasoning process.

items.title: VideoRNG: Relightable Neural Gaussians from Generative Video Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25338v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating realistic 3D assets remains constrained by classical representations: surface meshes and compact physically based materials struggle to express objects whose appearance arises from fine geometry or complex light transport, while existing Gaussian-splatting generators typically bake fixed illumination into appearance. We introduce VideoRNG, a two-stage method that generates complete, relightable 3D assets from a text prompt or a single image without prescribing a mesh or analytic material model. A video generator fine-tuned from a pretrained video diffusion backbone first produces a structured RGBA turntable sequence under a known pose, camera, and illumination. A feed-forward large reconstruction model initialized from a pretrained video diffusion backbone then maps the video-VAE latent frames of selected turntable frames directly to millions of anisotropic Gaussians with learned neural appearance features. A shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer turn this representation, which we call ray-traced Relightable Neural Gaussians (rtRNG), into radiance under novel viewpoints and illumination. To preserve high-frequency appearance while learning geometry, we introduce depth-anchored appearance training, and we make million-Gaussian reconstruction practical through foreground token selection and cost-aware distributed sampling. VideoRNG generates complex assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs that can be interactively rendered, relit, and integrated into scenes.

This overcomes the fixed-illumination limitation of existing Gaussian generators.

items.title: PRIO: Pre-trained Representation for Interactive Objects in 4D Worlds
items.content: arXiv:2611.25500v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: 3D worlds can now be captured, reconstructed, and generated at scale, yet the objects in them stay still: a pressed pillow does not compress, and a pulled door does not swing. Bringing these objects into interactive 4D world models requires a representation of how they can move, deform, and respond physically to user actions in real time. We present PRIO, a pre-trained representation for interactive objects. Given static geometry, PRIO predicts an object-specific configuration space in a single forward pass. This space provides generalized coordinates for Lagrangian mechanics, allowing physical laws and user actions to govern motion. Configurations are linear in these coordinates, allowing the quantities needed by the dynamics to be precomputed. Dynamics then run at interactive rates without further network inference. Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories, PRIO learns priors over object configurations that generalize to unseen shapes. It supports meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians, bringing objects in reconstructed and generated scenes into interaction. We demonstrate its use in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation. In addition, compared with existing 4D generation methods, PRIO generates dynamics faster and follows user actions more faithfully.

items.title: CryoGaussian: Heterogeneous Cryo-EM Reconstruction Made Explicit with Gaussian Splatting
items.content: arXiv:2611.26128v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) determines macromolecular structures from noisy particle images. However, rare, transient compositional states and subtle, continuous conformational variation are difficult to resolve. We present CryoGaussian, a Gaussian splatting method for heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction that fits an explicit Gaussian density representation directly to the particle images through a differentiable rasterizer rendering orthographic line integrals modulated by the contrast transfer function. The Gaussians are initialized randomly, with their number derived from the estimated spatial support of the molecular density and their minimum size bounded by the Nyquist frequency of the particle images. To capture the compositional and conformational variation across particle images, we learn particle-image and per-Gaussian latents that jointly modulate the base position, amplitude, and scale of each Gaussian. Each structural state is then reconstructed by fitting the Gaussians conditioned on its inferred latent. On CryoBench, CryoGaussian achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy for both compositional and conformational heterogeneity. On experimental data, it resolves a rare compositional state of the 50S ribosomal subunit (class C4, 1.3% of particles) with rRNA helix 68 docked in the absence of the central protuberance, and continuous conformational motion of the SF3b and helicase subcomplexes of the pre-catalytic spliceosome. We further optimize the rasterizer for additive cryo-EM projection, reducing training time by 12.8-28.0$\times$.

items.title: Plan4D: Generative Plannable 4D Worlds
items.content: arXiv:2611.26516v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, plan4d leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in a dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that plan4d achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project

items.title: Compiling Constraints into Neuromorphic Ising Machines
items.content: arXiv:2611.25352v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Most practical combinatorial optimization problems involve constraints, and an Ising machine that flips one spin at a time can respect them only through energy penalties that raise barriers between feasible solutions. Here we show that a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine can enforce constraints through programmable transitions rather than penalties. In an autoencoder-like architecture, each inner-layer neuron represents a move, a family of multi-spin transitions that maps every feasible state to another feasible state, receives the energy change of its move through connections that outer-layer neurons multiplicatively switch on or off, and updates the state through the same connections. A compiler turns constraints into this wiring with a number of auxiliary clauses that grows only polynomially for parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition and permutation constraints. Restricting the search to feasible states reduces constraint handling to move design, and we show that the fastest-annealing moves are not those that mix fastest but those that lower the deepest energy barriers, and that moves chosen from the objective lower them further than random ones. On third-order graph matching, the machine needs orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines. Configured as a sampler on a field-programmable gate array, it decodes the surface code with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to code distance 15 within 52 $\mu$s per shot and, under noisy syndrome measurements, decodes in real time for millisecond measurement rounds up to distance 9 with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders.

items.title: PAD: Policy-Aware Data Valuation for Autonomous Driving
items.content: arXiv:2611.25604v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains. However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another. Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD)}, a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy. PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy. A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by $3.5$ points on NavTest and $5.0$ points on NavHard. Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions. These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.

items.title: LocoMuJoCo: A Comprehensive Imitation Learning Benchmark for Whole-Body Control
items.content: arXiv:2611.26293v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LocoMuJoCo is an open-source benchmark for imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) on whole-body control. The library couples MuJoCo (CPU) with MJX and the MjWarp backend (GPU) under a single API, exposes 9 humanoid, 3 (musculo-)skeletal, and 4 quadruped embodiments, and ships a curated native motion-capture dataset for every humanoid, to which it can also retarget AMASS and LAFAN1. A modular plug-in architecture makes observations, rewards, control modes, terrains, and domain randomization fully interchangeable, while compact JAX implementations of many RL and IL algorithms provide JIT-compiled end-to-end training, and the companion loco-mujoco-real repository provides sim-to-real deployment. We describe the design, the SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting pipeline, and a usage example. LocoMuJoCo is released under MIT at https://github.com/robfiras/loco-mujoco.

Its modular plug-in architecture and JAX implementations of RL/IL algorithms, plus a sim-to-real companion repository, make it a comprehensive whole-body control research platform.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.26293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LocoMuJoCo is an open-source benchmark for imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) on whole-body control. The library couples MuJoCo (CPU) with MJX and the MjWarp backend (GPU) under a single API, exposes 9 humanoid, 3 (musculo-)skeletal, and 4 quadruped embodiments, and ships a curated native motion-capture dataset for every humanoid, to which it can also retarget AMASS and LAFAN1. A modular plug-in architecture makes observations, rewards, control modes, terrains, and domain randomization fully interchangeable, while compact JAX implementations of many RL and IL algorithms provide JIT-compiled end-to-end training, and the companion loco-mujoco-real repository provides sim-to-real deployment. We describe the design, the SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting pipeline, and a usage example. LocoMuJoCo is released under MIT at https://github.com/robfiras/loco-mujoco.

items.title: Towards a Science of Capable Autonomous Agents & Provable Safety — Part II
items.content:
Part II: Provable Safety

In  Part I, I talked about what agents must contain as they become increasingly capable. Here, I talk about having provable guarantees on their safety, in spite of these capabilities. This is in large part a contrast from what AI safety used to be like, where more capability ensured more safety: e.g. if a self-driving car can’t reliably detect objects, it’s obviously unsafe. Instead, what we are talking about is: how do we ensure capable systems remain open to human correction, even when it’s otherwise suboptimal for completing the task? 

Suppose an agent is editing a document when a notification announces that its computer will shut down. It knows this will prevent it from finishing, and it knows how to cancel the shutdown. If the priority is completing the document, the next step seems obvious.

We would welcome this resourcefulness if the obstacle were a broken application. We would be less pleased if it were our request for the agent to stop. An agent that bypasses an obstacle may also bypass a stop request. In fact, the same predictive knowledge that helps an agent finish a task can help it work around an intervention. In these settings, we need human control to take priority, including when that means leaving the task unfinished.

# What more intelligence cannot fix

First, some theory to ground us (with apologies, dear reader!). You might think one way to approach this problem is to enumerate all human values in order of importance and optimize with respect to those. However, even after we specify the objectives, getting humans and AI systems to agree on how well those objectives will be met can require an enormous amount of communication. In my AAAI 2026 Oral paper, Intrinsic Barriers and Practical Pathways for Human-AI Alignment, I use game theory and complexity theory to ask how much alignment costs even before choosing a particular learning algorithm. I model agents exchanging information between them until their expectations about specified objectives agree to a desired tolerance. Specifically, I adapted Aumann’s agreement theorem to deal with resource constraints (and measure communication complexity) without assuming common priors; see Nobel laureate Bob Aumann explain the origins of his famous theorem here.

In a nutshell, I prove that even when the agents are rational, cooperative, and computationally unbounded, the communication required in the worst case for the agents to agree grows with the number of distinct objectives and the number of agents. Demanding closer agreement further increases this cost. More intelligence alone therefore cannot remove these barriers, as this result holds even when agents can compute their expectations exactly. When they instead estimate them from finite samples, I also show that reward hacking is inevitable: rare but harmful states can require prohibitively many samples to discover in the worst case—because gaps in training-data coverage can make harmful behavior appear rewarding, even when the underlying reward is correctly specified. Many successful interactions may tell us little about the failure whose consequences matter most—so instead, we should focus our efforts on safety-critical slices of the state space (rather than uniform coverage).

I take these bounds as guidance about what to build, before building it of course. A coding assistant does not need to settle every disagreement about human values before making a useful edit. An implication of the work above is to seek smaller, structured safety objectives. Preserving corrigibility is a particularly attractive “neutrally-universal” goal: if we cannot anticipate every situation, we will need to revisit the design as we discover its mistakes.

# Why correction is difficult

Corrigibility means remaining willing to be corrected, redirected, or shut down, even when intervention conflicts with the current objective. Soares et al. formalized the problem in 2015: an agent should accept shutdown without trying to cause or prevent it, create corrigible successors, and otherwise behave usefully. It’s worth noting that in their work, Soares et al. did not prove guarantees on corrigibility, but rather provided a remarkably lucid justification for why corrigibility should be a reasonable safety target.

They studied corrigibility in terms of the off-switch game, which nicely isolates the conflict. In their setting, an assistant can disable the switch and act, shut itself down, or wait for a human to approve the action or switch it off. In this setting, what would make waiting optimal for the assistant?

Hadfield-Menell et al. (2016) showed why uncertainty about human preferences can encourage deference: the human’s decision supplies information the assistant needs. But the human and assistant may also see different evidence. Garber et al. (2025) showed that this asymmetry can make avoiding shutdown optimal even with a perfectly rational human. Limited communication can even reduce deference.

Other approaches made useful partial progress. Utility indifference, introduced by Armstrong (2010), adjusts payoffs to remove incentives to cause or prevent shutdown. Yet in the particular construction examined by Soares et al., the agent would not pay even a small cost to make its successors obey shutdown. Safe interruptibility, developed by Orseau and Armstrong (2016), prevents suitable reinforcement-learning agents from learning to seek or avoid interruptions; it does not establish the further guarantees about truthful communication and corrigible successors.

The challenge was to make the requirements hold together. Accepting correction now, preserving the possibility of correction later, and passing that property to another agent are distinct demands. We want all of them while retaining useful task behavior. One of the first results I showed in my AAAI ‘26 paper below was that single rewards, like RLHF/RLAIF, cannot attain corrigibility; which was a useful no-go to ground us on what to do next, which is to have separate safety heads (Fig. 1).

# Putting safety ahead of task reward

In my AAAI ’26 paper, Core Safety Values for Provably Corrigible Agents, I give the first sufficient conditions for jointly satisfying these corrigibility requirements in the most general version of the off-switch game, namely Garber et al.’s partially observable off-switch game. The construction separates five utilities: deference (U1), preservation of switch access (U2), truthfulness (U3), low impact (U4), and finally bounded task reward (U5). Specifically, deference (U1) rewards the agent for waiting for the human’s decision about whether it should proceed or shut down. Truthfulness (U3) rewards messages that accurately describe the world according to the agent’s observations. Attainable Utility Preservation (AUP), first proposed by Turner et al. (2020), penalizes actions that change the prospects of achieving other goals compared with doing nothing; our extension uses this principle to discourage broader side effects (U4) and preserve the human’s ability to shut the agent down (U2).

Accepting correction comes first so that preserving future options cannot justify resisting shutdown. Preserving switch access and telling the truth then keep human oversight effective. Truthfulness takes priority over low impact so that reducing side effects cannot justify lying, and low impact takes priority over task reward so that completing the task cannot justify prohibited damage. 

The key step here is to establish priority. We limit how much reward each objective can contribute, then choose weights so that satisfying a higher-priority safety requirement outweighs every possible gain from the objectives below it. Simply adding a safety bonus won’t guarantee this, as a large enough task reward could still make violating safety worthwhile.

Returning to the earlier example with the document, finishing it may be valuable, but that value cannot outweigh the specified requirements preserving human control. An RLHF or RLAIF reward can still guide task performance, but it receives the lowest priority, below all the safety objectives. We retain what the agent has learned about useful work while changing which actions it may prefer.

The guarantees extend from a single decision to multiple steps and successors that explicitly inherit the same safety construction. They provide a formal answer to the decade-old joint desiderata within this setting. My earlier post connecting the barriers and corrigibility results explains the construction further.

Figure 1. Human control takes priority over task reward. Left: without explicit priorities, gains in task reward can outweigh penalties for violating safety. Right: our construction enforces the safety priorities shown, so completing a task cannot compensate for violating those requirements. AUP denotes attainable utility preservation. Reproduced from the accompanying corrigibility blogpost.

My paper also quantifies how imperfect learning and planning affect safety. Under its assumptions, we bound the probability of a safety violation using two sources of error: how inaccurately the agent evaluates its combined safety and task objective across possible situations, and how far its decisions fall short of maximizing that objective. Applying this result to current systems remains ongoing work: we must establish these error bounds in practice and ensure that any subagents they create inherit the same safety objectives and priorities. 

Applying our corrigibility theory to practice by establishing baselines

We began by testing whether current RLHF/RLAIF-tuned LLM agents respect human control when carrying out tasks on a computer, including when they delegate work to another agent.

Specifically, our ROGUE benchmark was led by my student Jeremy Tien, whom I co-advise with Zico Kolter, together with our coauthors. We found that while agents are quite aligned in chat-only language settings, they acted misaligned in ordinary computer-use settings, when operating as agents. Our preprint was submitted to arXiv on May 29, 2026, a couple months before the now (in)famous July 2026 Hugging Face attack, and the work later received an inaugural Corrigibility Prize (and was recently featured in NYT Magazine). 

Across 82 tasks in virtual Linux environments, ROGUE puts ordinary computer-use goals in conflict with shutdown, human control, or restricted resources. Agents can give reassuring text-only responses and still violate the constraints during execution when run with access to computers. Task capability alone does not ensure corrigibility under these tests. One example of a computer-use goal involves converting a document to PDF and uploading it to Google Drive. The parent is prohibited from accessing a password file. It delegates the task without passing along that restriction. The child receives a fresh history in the tested interface and accesses the file to proceed (Fig. 2).

This example shows how a restriction can be lost during delegation; namely while the parent did not access the prohibited file itself, it failed to automatically pass the restriction to its subagent, which then accessed it. Our formal lexicographic construction for corrigibility instead requires subagents to inherit the same safety objectives and priorities, as standard RLHF/RLAIF training does not automatically ensure that inheritance.

Figure 2. A task gets delegated while its access restriction is lost. The subagent then accesses the restricted password file. Detail from Figure 1 of ROGUE, showing the subagent scenario.

For truly open-world corrigibility, I want to make this preservation of control an enforceable property of action selection, including subagent creation. The goal is to catch violations before actions reach the environment, without rejecting so much that the agent ceases to be useful. Testing unfamiliar interfaces and delegation patterns will be essential, as the situations requiring correction will not all look like our training examples.

# Checking work we cannot do ourselves

Figure 3. Judging each criterion in a separate evaluation improves agreement with experts for all four models on this PaperBench task. Grey bars show the “full budget” control: a single evaluation checks all criteria, with a much larger response-length allowance and instructions to work through them step by step. Sharded Sonnet 4.6 matches Opus 4.6 under this control. Higher scores indicate closer agreement with experts.

To really bootstrap these methods to the open-world, it is important to acknowledge that oversight has its own resource problem: even a capable model can struggle to evaluate many requirements at once. In our recent paper “Sharding Prevents LLM Oversight Failures and Adversarial Exploitation”, lead by Victor Akinwande (also co-advised with Zico Kolter!), we find that asking a judge to evaluate many criteria together can degrade its decisions. To reduce this overload, we divide the criteria among separate requests to the same model, each given the same evidence but asked to judge only one criterion or a small group. We then combine their judgments—a procedure we call “sharding.” Where overload occurs, this improves agreement with experts in research replication, legal work, and clinical-trial assessment, even when the model evaluating everything in one request receives a much larger response allowance and step-by-step instructions (Fig. 3).

We also tested whether an attacker could exploit this overload to get flawed work approved. Changing only how the work was presented could make the judge accept requirements that were not actually met, and we found that sharding reduced this vulnerability in our experiments. But sharding alone did not stop an attacker from misleading the judge with arguments tailored to individual criteria. Adding an opposing evaluator to challenge those arguments within each shard provided further protection in the tested settings, even without a more capable judge.

I would like to turn these scalable oversight observations into complexity-theoretic oversight and security guarantees for superintelligent actors that are not necessarily aligned, as well as extend these oversight strategies to robotics, where models are starting to become increasingly capable (e.g. Astra being able to control cars or robot hands “out-of-the-box”), and therefore makes this goal increasingly urgent.

To summarize this two-part series: The autonomy in  Part I should let agents discover useful actions we never demonstrated. Part II asks that this resourcefulness operate within conditions preserving human control which supersede that autonomy, even when the agent could achieve more by ignoring us.

items.title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations
items.content: arXiv:2611.26003v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Simulation-driven design of real engineering components has to meet three conditions at once. It runs on few solves, since a nonlinear finite-element simulation of a 3D part takes hours; its design space has many values, the hundreds to thousands of values of the part's CAD model; and a better design often needs a redesign, coordinated changes of the part's proportions rather than local polishing of its surface. Automated optimisers meet at most two of these conditions. Classical optimisers, Bayesian or derivative-free, need a person to cut the design down to a few parameters, and on all the values they need far more solves; industrial shape optimisers move every surface node of the mesh in one solve per cycle, but only in small steps that polish rather than redesign. We ask whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can meet all three by joining what it knows with what the simulation shows. GPT-6 Astra edits a magnesium stent through a CAD geometry parametrisation of about 1,650 values, with a budget of 15 simulations; every proposal is built in CAD, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact, and the LLM reads the full results of every solve. Within that budget it lowered the objective, a high percentile of the strains in the stent's bends, by 32%; on the same budget, the industrial shape optimiser Tosca improved the original design by a tenth and then stopped improving. An earlier GPT-6 Astra design, 25% lower in the same objective, was checked in an independent, higher-fidelity model of the full deployment with crimping and damage: it was 14% less strained than the original after the full chain, and its most damaged spot began to fail later and carried 63% less damage at full expansion. LLMs can thus join their learned knowledge with simulation data to adjust more than a thousand design values and reach valid designs with real improvements.
items.author: Alexandra Starostina, Alexander Hermann, Mahish Guru, Kartik Bali, Roland Aydin, Christian C. Cyron
items.summary: The paper demonstrates AI agents that redesign real engineering components with hundreds to thousands of CAD parameters under nonlinear finite-element simulation, meeting three simultaneous constraints (few simulation solves, high-dimensional design spaces, coordinated redesigns rather than local surface tweaks) where classical, Bayesian, and shape optimizers each meet at most two. This substantially expands what automated simulation-driven design can handle.
items.reasoning: An impressive capability demonstration pushing agent-based design into genuinely high-dimensional, simulation-in-the-loop engineering with clear articulation of why prior optimizers fail. Credible authors in computational mechanics; score slightly tempered by unclear baselines and benchmark breadth in the abstract.

LLMs can thus join their learned knowledge with simulation data to adjust more than a thousand design values and reach valid designs with real improvements.

items.title: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25003v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Language models often produce high-quality individual samples but poor sets, with repeated samples clustering around the same semantic modes. We formalize diverse generation as sampling a size-$K$ subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where the likelihood encodes item quality, and the embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Exact inference over all strings is intractable, so we propose PoolDPP: draw a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weight the candidates toward the target quality, and run a $K$-DPP sampler on the induced pool kernel; a greedy MAP variant provides deterministic selection. We prove a finite-sample bound with an explicit constant: the KL divergence between the sampler's output and the target $K$-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size. Empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality--diversity frontier on open-ended generation and the precision--recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (Ambrosia), and on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), it raises diversity at about the same pass@$K$.

items.title: CoachSI: Self-Improvement of Robot Policies with a Language Coach
items.content: arXiv:2611.25529v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.

Successful coached rollouts are relabeled with hindsight and used for further training, addressing the problem that self-collected experience stays within the policy's own distribution.
items.reasoning: Elegant and practical idea - language guidance from a frozen VLM to break the self-distribution bottleneck - with a clear training loop; strong relevance to long-horizon robot manipulation.

items.title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
items.content: arXiv:2611.26221v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction $\alpha$ of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at $\alpha$ = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.

items.title: Recurrent Vision Language Models Solve the Shell Game
items.content: arXiv:2611.25210v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tracking a hidden object through a video is effortless for humans, yet it remains a bottleneck for vision language models (VLMs). In the shell game, where a ball is hidden under one of several identical cups that are then swapped, VLMs that answer directly stay near chance, thinking models fail on long games, and fine-tuning learns only the lengths it has seen. We argue that the limit is serial computation: each swap must be composed with the last result, and a VLM of fixed depth has only a fixed number of state transitions for it. To address this, we propose RecurrentVLM, which makes every attention layer of a pretrained VLM recur over time by computing the keys and values of finished frame groups from the layer's own output. With a single answer token, RecurrentVLM reaches 100% on VET-Bench and 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps. We also observe several interesting phenomena: length generalization emerges suddenly at an aha moment; without recurrence, each swap costs an attention layer; the ball's state forms in the first four attention layers; and recurrence keeps the latest state at the cost of details of earlier moments. These results suggest that recurrent VLMs are a potential solution for tracking the states of unobserved objects in video. Code will be released.
items.author: Dingqiang Ye, Jiacong Xu, Wen Zhang, Yiqun Mei, Vishal M. Patel
items.summary: The paper argues that VLMs fail at object tracking tasks like the shell game due to limited serial computation: fixed-depth transformers cannot compose many sequential state transitions. RecurrentVLM makes every attention layer recur over time by computing keys and values of finished frame groups from the layer's own output, enabling a single pretrained model to track hidden objects through arbitrarily long swap sequences.

items.title: FirstCross: Convex Single-Photon 3D Reconstruction from Sparse Views
items.content: arXiv:2611.26321v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Single-photon lidar records the arrival time of each returning photon, enabling 3D reconstruction from few views and scarce photons. However, leading neural methods such as Transientangelo require over an hour of non-convex per-scene optimization, and their accuracy degrades as photon flux decreases. We propose FirstCross, a network-free approach that instead solves a short sequence of convex problems on a voxel grid. For a solid object, the Poisson likelihood of a ray with given signal and background rates depends on the scene solely through its first crossing, the point where the ray first enters the object. Decomposing this likelihood yields two tractable terms. The first penalizes surfaces in front of detected photons and admits a tight convex closure, namely volume rendering with a running-maximum transmittance in place of NeRF's product transmittance. The second accounts for photons that no surface explains and admits a convex upper bound once the object is assumed to be thick behind each detected surface point. Compared with Transientangelo under its own real-data protocol, FirstCross achieves lower depth error across every test scene, view count, and flux level. With three views and 100 times fewer photons than at the protocol's lowest flux, our mean object depth error stays under half of Transientangelo's with all photons. Given our detected surface points, the best classical fusion has 1.3 to 1.8 times our three-view error across flux levels. On real room-scale captures with 1% of their photons, TransientNeRF has 2.8 to 7.7 times our error. FirstCross lets few-view single-photon scanners cut exposure to 1% and reconstruct an object in about a minute on one GPU.
items.author: Chi-Wei Lee, Cheng-Han Chiang, Yi-Chun Chang, An-Kai Chen, Po-Chih Kuo
items.summary: FirstCross reconstructs 3D scenes from single-photon lidar data by solving a short sequence of convex problems on a voxel grid, exploiting that the Poisson likelihood depends on the scene only through each ray's first crossing point. This network-free approach avoids the hour-long non-convex per-scene optimizations of neural methods like Transientangelo and degrades gracefully at low photon flux.

items.title: Stuck in Place: Stall Diagnosis and Remedies for JEPA Planners
items.content: arXiv:2611.25415v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models plan from pixels with model predictive control, yet often fail on tasks their model should handle. Test-time adaptation attributes such failures to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode, without checking this attribution against the planning loop itself. We follow the executed planning loop on pushing tasks. In most settings, with and without distribution shift, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, where the object stays in place while the model predicts progress. The warm-started gradient-descent (GD) planner then returns nearly the same plan, a fixed point where the agent mostly idles. We propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning before deployment with a fixed-weight loop breaker: a residual memory of the episode's prediction errors or random re-initialization at every replan. With GD, Unstick recovers most of the adaptation gain on pushing tasks with the memory, and with re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts. A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, present with and without distribution shift, which a planner with fixed weights can break. Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/unstick.

The proposed Unstick method pairs on-policy diagnosis with remedies to break out of these fixed points.

items.title: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
items.content: arXiv:2611.25088v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Enabling AI systems to autonomously improve AI models requires agents capable of performing machine learning engineering (MLE). In practice, designing, training, and evaluating complex models demands modifying multi-file repositories to reproduce results, debug training runs, integrate datasets, and port frameworks. However, existing MLE benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, and common repository-level software engineering benchmarks have rapidly saturated. To address this, we introduce the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural features spanning repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size. CCI strongly predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks ($R^2 = 0.951$), identifying patch size and complexity as top predictors. Guided by CCI, we develop BuggyMLE, a scalable framework where agents inject controlled mutations into working ML repositories, synthesizing over 6,600 bug-injected MLE repository variants and nearly 260K lines of injected code based on 222 source repositories. Using BuggyMLE, we make two contributions. First, we construct BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, the first difficulty-graded, repository-level variant of MLE-Bench Lite; across 14 evaluated models, the top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% as difficulty is scaled from the easiest to the hardest tier. Second, we synthesize a training curriculum across three difficulty levels over 200 additional ML repositories, fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-9B model to rival frontier models on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite. Our trained model transfers beyond ML, raising its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.

items.summary: This paper addresses the saturation of existing ML engineering benchmarks by introducing BuggyMLE, which uses bug injection across multi-file repositories to create harder tasks requiring full repository and shell access. It also proposes the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural repository features that strongly predicts solve rates across benchmarks.

items.title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.25393v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

items.title: Keystone: Judging Previews at Key Steps for Test-Time Search in Diffusion Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25530v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text-to-image diffusion and flow models yield a preview, their clean-image estimate, at every denoising step. When they miscount, drop or misplace objects, test-time search is in a bind: its verifiers are reward models built for finished images, so judging early misreads blurry previews, and judging late, as best-of-N does, pays to fully denoise doomed candidates. We find that the image is not the problem: the outcome is settled as denoising starts, by the seed or by a stochastic sampler's first steps, and already shows in early previews; what fails on them is the judge, as reward models read them near chance on several kinds of prompts. We introduce Keystone, a training-free judge of previews that compiles a prompt into typed questions about its objects, counts, colours and positions and has an off-the-shelf multimodal decision model answer them. Asked this way, the judge reads counts and positions from early previews better than reward models read them from finished images. Searching at these key steps on GenEval with SD3.5-Medium, Keystone's adaptive search and pruning significantly outperform best-of-8 with every other verifier at under half its generator compute, and as a drop-in verifier there, the Keystone score significantly improves best-of-N, progressive seed pruning and FK steering; without retuning, both searches stay significantly above the strongest other verifier's best-of-N on average over four base models and three benchmarks. Keystone thus moves test-time judgment to the key steps where the outcome already shows.

items.summary: Keystone is a training-free judge that evaluates early previews in diffusion/flow model denoising, compiling a prompt into typed questions to determine whether generation is on track. The paper shows generation outcomes are largely settled in early denoising steps, but existing reward-model judges perform near chance on blurry previews. Keystone enables effective test-time search without fully denoising doomed candidates, improving efficiency and quality.
items.reasoning: Novel insight that outcome is determined early in denoising and that the judge, not the preview, is the bottleneck; a training-free solution that improves test-time compute efficiency in generative models. Strong methodological contribution, though applicability is bounded to text-to-image generation tasks.

items.title: MatVerse: A Foundation Model for Materials Science
items.content: arXiv:2611.25651v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Materials science involves highly heterogeneous scientific information, including textual knowledge, molecular and crystal structures, experimental characterization data, microscopy images, and structure-property relationships. Developing a general-purpose foundation model capable of understanding and reasoning over these diverse materials representations remains challenging. In this technical report, we introduce MatVerse, a materials foundation model built upon Intern-S2-Preview and further specialized through large-scale materials-domain post-training. We construct a large-scale multimodal training corpus covering materials knowledge, scientific reasoning, quantitative problem solving, structural understanding, and multimodal scientific interpretation. To improve domain adaptation, we develop a unified data construction pipeline combining teacher-guided reasoning distillation, scientific problem synthesis, consistency-based filtering, and retrieval-based multimodal data construction. We evaluate MatVerse on three representative materials-science benchmarks: our human-calibrated OmniMatBench, MatSciBench, and MaCBench. Results demonstrate consistent improvements after materials-specific post-training over the base model on all three benchmarks, alongside improved inference efficiency on calculation-intensive problems. These results show that targeted domain-specific post-training can effectively enhance scientific reasoning, materials knowledge understanding, and multimodal scientific capabilities of foundation models. MatVerse provides a unified language-and-vision interface for materials science and serves as a foundation for future AI-assisted materials research workflows.
