items.title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining
items.content: arXiv:2611.25926v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7% and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.
items.author: Jeff Duan, Matt Thomson
items.summary: ROAM-GRPO augments GRPO-based RLVR post-training to counter mode collapse in reasoning policies: well-solved problems are routed to an off-mode track where the model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies, incentivizing exploration of diverse reasoning paths. The goal is to preserve pass@k performance and output creativity that typically degrade as policies converge to a single mode.
items.reasoning: Targets the well-documented diversity collapse problem in RLVR post-training, a hot and important topic, with a concrete algorithmic mechanism. The idea is timely and plausible; score reflects strong relevance but uncertainty about breadth of benchmarks and magnitude of gains.

items.title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
items.content: arXiv:2611.26248v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.
items.author: Yang Wan, Linchao Zhu
items.summary: TwinLab-Bench evaluates AI scientists on fully self-designed experiments across 52 tasks from physical sciences, life sciences, and engineering, executing agent-designed protocols against readings grounded in real laboratories. It goes beyond existing benchmarks that only test executing given workflows or choosing among predefined candidate measurements, supporting the most open ability of experimental design.
items.reasoning: Grounding agentic experiment design in real lab execution rather than simulation is a genuinely harder and underexplored evaluation frontier, with broad coverage of tasks; score reflects novelty and importance of the benchmark for AI-scientist research.

items.title: LLM GerryMandering: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects in LLM Audits
items.content: arXiv:2611.26538v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Intersectional bias arises when a model treats people who hold several marginalised identities at once differently from what their separate identities would predict. Auditing such intersectional subgroups remains a challenge: their number grows quadratically, and there is no agreed baseline for what independent attributes would predict. Without such a baseline, many existing audits flag a subgroup when it exceeds each attribute alone, a condition that attributes acting independently already satisfy. We test this standard criterion on 150 synthetic datasets built with no interaction. With the shuffle null, it flags 66.1 false subgroups per dataset on average, and at least one in every dataset. When we plant interactions of known size into these datasets, a repaired null lets the criterion recover only 32% of them. We introduce ADDIS (Additive Intersectional Screen), which fits an additive model over all attributes, scores each subgroup by its Additive Residual Distance (ARD) from that model's prediction, and tests it against a Freedman-Lane null. On our synthetic benchmark, ADDIS flags 0.09 false subgroups per dataset and recovers 84% of the same planted interactions. We then build IndiPersona, 10,000 synthetic Indian personas with six identity attributes, and audit 13 open language models. The standard criterion flags 7.1% of the 738 tested subgroups on average; ADDIS flags 3.0%. Gender identity crossed with sexual orientation is the largest pairing in every model, and counterfactual personas confirm it and additionally reveal a caste x class interaction in all but one model that the observational test lacked the data to detect. Much of what audits report as intersectional bias can thus arise from independent single-attribute effects alone, yet a small core of interactions survives.
items.author: George Rahul, Ronit Jahilal, Bhaskara Hanuma Vedula, Ponnurangam Kumaraguru, Pushkar Shukla
items.summary: Tackles intersectional bias auditing in LLMs by proposing a principled baseline separating genuine attribute interactions from additive effects, using a shuffle null. Shows the common criterion of exceeding per-attribute bias flags large numbers of false subgroups on synthetic datasets with no interaction (averaging 66.1 false flags per dataset). Provides a methodological correction with direct implications for fairness audits.
items.reasoning: Identifies and quantifies a serious statistical flaw in prevailing bias-audit practice and offers a corrective methodology validated on controlled synthetic data. High relevance for AI fairness and safety auditing, though applied scope is evaluation methodology rather than a new capability.

items.title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.25123v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.
items.author: Ziyan Yang, Taiwei Shi, Jieyu Zhao
items.summary: GrepMem proposes a deliberately simple memory mechanism for long-horizon LLM agents: an append-only plain-text log of the full interaction history plus a regex search tool for on-demand recall, avoiding lossy summarization or pre-built indexes. By preserving everything and deferring retrieval decisions to query time, it sidesteps the problem of guessing what future tasks will need. The approach challenges the trend toward increasingly complex structured agent memory systems.
items.reasoning: Counterintuitive, pragmatic idea with broad applicability to the fast-growing agent memory area. Simplicity is both a strength and a limitation; the lossless claim is compelling but scalability of regex recall over very long histories is a question.

items.title: From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware
items.content: arXiv:2611.25339v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As LLM agents increasingly generate RTL alongside the tests and reviews that validate it, self-generated evidence is a weak foundation for trustworthy hardware. We present our seven-stage verification-gated workflow, evolved during a post-quantum design port, in which a gate counts only if shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants, and reviewer agents audit work before commit. We then audit this evidence with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The flow ported an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card: all six operations are byte-exact on the board, and it passes all 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases (of 285) and 484 ML-DSA known answers. However, passing module tests overstate the verification strength. Across three RTL modules, existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants; specification-derived tests guided by the survivors raise the fresh-draw decapsulation kill rate from 48% to 74%. In pre-registered single-model replays on flaws invisible to known-answer tests, undirected whole-design review catches two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions, whereas module-scoped review catches every known flaw in all 54 sessions. Even scoped review detects planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks (one added for the replay) flag every one. In this study, trustworthy agentic hardware needed author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.
items.author: Jungmin Park, Eunha Kim, Wooseop Kim, Seongjoon Cho, Byungho Cha
items.summary: This paper presents a seven-stage verification-gated LLM-agent workflow for porting post-quantum cryptography to FPGA hardware, where each gate must be shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants before it counts as evidence. The flow successfully ported ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ card passing all applicable NIST ACVP cases, yet the audit with netlist mutants and formal checks still reveals what tests and agent reviews miss. Its central contribution is a rigorous epistemology for trusting self-generated AI hardware evidence.

items.title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills
items.content: arXiv:2611.25429v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

This targeted approach improves on prior self-evolution methods that judge runs only by outcome.
items.reasoning: Novel application of coverage-guided testing ideas to agent skill self-improvement; the instruction-level attribution is a clear methodological advance for the agent-skills area.

items.title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
items.content: arXiv:2611.25605v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

items.title: Safe Subgame Resolving in Multiplayer Games
items.content: arXiv:2611.25981v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Poker and other games with hidden information are too large to solve in one pass. Strong systems compute a complete blueprint strategy offline and refine it in real time inside the reached subgame. In 2p0s games, a safety theorem guarantees that subgame resolving never increases how much an adversary can gain by exploiting the resolved strategy relative to the blueprint strategy. With three or more players acting independently, no such guarantee exists yet, and heuristic resolving can increase the profile's best-response gap. We prove the first conditional safety theorem for uncorrelated multiplayer subgame resolving, a post-hoc certificate for any delivered update. The best-response gap of the resolved profile exceeds that of the blueprint by at most four terms. Two concern the resolver: the subgame value the blueprint promised without realizing ($A_i^{S}$) and the resolver's subgame solve error ($\varepsilon_i$). The other two are the opponents' best-response gains inside the subgame over their promised values ($\sum_q M_{q}$) and a structural tax ($\Theta$), which measures how much the players' total utility can change. The tax is zero in constant-sum games, including every rake-free poker variant. Constructions attain each term with equality. On three-player Leduc poker and on Kuhn poker with up to six players, resolving without a certificate raises the gap beyond a small tolerance in 12% to 100% of the updates. The certificate flags every such update and accepts 41% (Kuhn) and 86% (Leduc) of the standard resolving updates. A resolver that keeps the blueprint whenever the certificate exceeds the tolerance delivers no harmful update. The certificate needs only one best-response pass per opponent inside the subgame, so real-time multiplayer solvers that refine a blueprint can attach it as a safety check. Code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/MultiPlayerSolver

items.title: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
items.content: arXiv:2611.26286v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.
items.author: Ilya Gusev
items.summary: This study measures claim-level overlap in peer reviews, finding critique homogenization rising sharply (e.g., ICLR overlap from 12.0% to 21.3% between 2026 and 2027), with similar trends at NeurIPS, ICML, and journals. Applying the MELD LLM-text detector, it shows LLM-flagged reviews overlap with other reviews significantly more than unflagged ones. This provides quantitative evidence that LLM use is reducing the diversity of problems caught in peer review, threatening a core mechanism of scientific quality control.
items.reasoning: Timely and important empirical measurement of LLM impact on the scientific peer review ecosystem, with a large multi-venue corpus and a clever detector-correlation analysis. Single-author work and reliance on a flagging detector introduce some uncertainty, but the topic has broad significance.

items.title: Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25119v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Learned weather models are experimentally accessible computational systems whose internal representations can be inspected and manipulated. Using sparse autoencoder features from GraphCast, DeepMind's autoregressive weather forecasting model, we test whether causal relevance requires physical semantics, a question that matters for auditing whether AI forecasters used in high-assurance settings rely on reliable mechanisms. We also look at whether physically associated latent directions can be steered to improve extreme-event forecasts, where interventions are applied to the model's internal activations during the rollout. We find that ablating a feature locked to GraphCast's computational mesh increases global geopotential height error despite lacking conventional physical semantics. Second, suppressing convection- and low-level-vorticity-associated features weakens predicted tropical-cyclone deepening (the fall in central pressure during intensification), while amplifying them reduces intensity error, with amplification of convection features through feature scaling achieving a median of 51\% error reduction over seven storms. Together, these results separate interpretable, physical association from causal utility and establish sparse features as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening on learned weather dynamics.

items.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
items.content: arXiv:2611.25403v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

items.title: LIFT: Latent Flow Matching for Probabilistic Cell Fate Dynamics with Single Cell Snapshots
items.content: arXiv:2611.25917v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Lineage tracing links cell states through clonal ancestry, but does not generally identify unique source-descendant pairings. Learning from such data therefore requires a model of conditional outcomes, rather than only the terminal population distribution. We introduce LIFT, a latent flow framework for probabilistic cell-state generation from lineage-informed couplings. Variational inference encodes alternative outcomes in a latent space, while a conditional prior enables sampling from the initial state alone. A Mean Flow decoder predicts future cell state directly, requiring one decoder evaluation per sampling, which makes it convenient to predict cell fate through large scale Monte-Carlo sampling. This construction combines a representation of one-to-many relationships with efficient sampling and an analysis of conditional prediction error. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate LIFT's ability to recover both population distribution and cell fate probabilities.

items.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
items.content: arXiv:2611.26059v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.

items.title: HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
items.content: arXiv:2611.26363v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.

items.title: VoxForge: A Unified Foundation Model for Dense 3D Features Across MRI, CT and PET
items.content: arXiv:2611.25309v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A unified 3D medical foundation model promises reusable, frozen features that serve a wide variety of tasks such as segmentation, classification and registration on MRI, CT and PET as well as specialist models do. Generalist models still need separate backbones for localized and global tasks, specialist models are confined to a single modality, with the concern that spanning modalities under-emphasizes fine anatomy, and both typically rely on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive. We present VoxForge, a single encoder that integrates recent advances in 3D architecture, self-distillation and cross-modal curricula to learn transferable features from permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes. We evaluate it strictly frozen, the test a reusable foundation model must pass, against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models on segmentation, classification and registration across MRI and CT, and on PET, which it never sees. VoxForge has the best or tied-best average rank in every task group, serves localized and global tasks across modalities at the level of state-of-the-art specialists, and is extremely label-efficient, matching top-performing models on TotalSegmentator CT with a tenth of the labels.

items.title: What One Sample Cannot See: Why Fewer Denoising Steps Can Score Higher on Physics Benchmarks
items.content: arXiv:2611.25632v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.
items.author: Yutao Li, Chen Wang
items.summary: This paper identifies a flaw in the Physics-IQ benchmark used to evaluate video generators as world models: comparing each generated video against a single ground-truth recording rewards reduced variation among sampled futures even when the underlying distribution becomes less accurate, explaining counterintuitive results where fewer denoising steps score better. The authors introduce Kernel Physics-IQ, which removes this bias in expectation using only two independent samples per condition, and validate it across five image-to-video models.
items.reasoning: Provides a rigorous, actionable critique of an increasingly used benchmark for video world models, with a clean mathematical decomposition and a practical fix. Relevant to a fast-growing evaluation area, though the scope is a single benchmark.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.25632v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.

items.title: Who Moved My $Z$ Boson? Revealing Resonance Features Inside a Neural Network
items.content: arXiv:2611.26291v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Methods used in mechanistic interpretability have revealed human-aligned concepts inside language and image models. In this paper, we search for physics concepts inside a neural a generative collider physics model trained on real LHC data (ShellFlow). We discover features inside ShellFlow that represent resonances, such as the $Z$, $J/\psi$, and $\Upsilon$. The network was never told which muons come from a resonance, it was only trained to generate the kinematics of the final-state particles. We use these features to alter aspects of the $Z$ boson: we change its mass between $\sim80$ and $105$ GeV, and removing such a feature from the neural network produces a broader $Z$ peak. In both cases the rest of the invariant mass spectrum remains mostly unchanged. The feature was built from the gradients of the neural network, and its selectivity was built using pattern recognition methods. A generative particle physics model trained on unlabeled data can be modified internally to change a physical quantity.

items.title: VR-SparseQuant: Accurate FP4 Quantization with 2:4 Sparsity on Vera Rubin
items.content: arXiv:2611.25717v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In recent years, GPUs have incorporated increasingly specialized support for low-precision computation, from Hopper's FP8 to Blackwell's FP4 Tensor Cores. Precision formats have evolved alongside this hardware, from MXFP4 and NVFP4 on Blackwell to E2M1 FP4 with direct UE5M3 block scaling on Vera Rubin, which we term as $\boldsymbol{VRFP4}$. These advances help serve larger language models at lower cost, but four-bit activation quantization can substantially degrade model quality. We introduce VR-SparseQuant, which uses Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 sparsity to recover accuracy while retaining native FP4 execution. By allowing two sparse streams to overlap, we use the same FP4 value budget as dense quantization to refine activations with larger errors. Offline scale-ratio calibration avoids runtime search, while a shared-weight GEMM accumulates both streams efficiently. On Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, VR-SparseQuant reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from $\boldsymbol{6.85}$ to $\boldsymbol{5.57}$ versus dense RTN W4A4. Including activation preparation, our native Rubin kernels for VRFP4 achieve up to $\boldsymbol{3.1\times}$ GEMM and $\boldsymbol{2.7\times}$ MoE speedup over BF16. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of adaptive activation quantization using Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 structured sparse FP4 instructions.

items.summary: This paper targets the accuracy loss of four-bit activation quantization by exploiting NVIDIA Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 structured sparsity alongside its E2M1 FP4 format with UE5M3 block scaling. By overlapping two sparse streams within the same FP4 value budget, VR-SparseQuant refines problematic activations while retaining native FP4 execution speed.

items.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
items.content: arXiv:2611.26510v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

items.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
items.content: arXiv:2611.26613v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

items.title: Text Lives in the Guidance: Preventing Silent Text Rewriting in Cached Diffusion Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2611.25382v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) now render long, legible text in images, and feature caching is a standard way to accelerate them. Caches are judged by image-level metrics, which do not check whether the rendered text is still correct. We find that caching silently rewrites this text. On Z-Image, TaylorSeer at 2.9x fewer FLOPs lowers word accuracy from 62% to 46%, while ImageReward and CLIP Score barely change. Sampling with fewer steps at the same compute keeps almost all of this text, so the loss comes from how the cache predicts the skipped steps. Decomposing the cache error along classifier-free guidance (CFG), we trace this loss mainly to the guidance term, the difference between the conditional and unconditional predictions, which caches extrapolate worst on text. Correcting the guidance inside the text alone recovers most of the lost text. We therefore propose GuideCache, which recomputes both CFG branches only on the tokens with the largest predicted guidance error, using the guidance terms that the cache already stores. At 2.4x fewer FLOPs, GuideCache restores full-compute prompt fidelity on Z-Image and Qwen-Image, and on Z-Image it renders text as well as or better than ToCa, TeaCache, and FasterCache while staying much closer to the full model's output. GuideCache works with caches of any order, and on top of fewer sampling steps it keeps more text than step reduction at a higher speedup. These results suggest that acceleration methods for text-rendering models should be evaluated on the text they render.

items.title: What's in the box? Revealing Object Layouts Inside Opaque Boxes via Contactless Vibration Excitation and Sensing
items.content: arXiv:2611.25728v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Can we reveal what is inside an opaque box by observing its surface vibrations? Objects inside a box alter its mechanical response, providing cues about their hidden locations. We introduce a method that uses these cues to predict a box's 2D occupancy layout entirely remotely. A nearby speaker excites vibrations, which we measure on one visible wall using a grid of laser points and a camera measuring each point's speckle-pattern shifts. Our model, WhisperBox, learns to encode these vibrations into a latent representation and decode it into an occupancy map of the box's contents. The method requires no physical contact to excite or sense vibrations. We demonstrate layout recovery across various boxes and single- and multiple-object scenes, with generalization to unseen object instances, positions, orientations, and weights, as well as changes in laser placement and excitation source. Our analysis reveals that informative frequency bands need not coincide with the box's resonances and that the learned latent space captures object placement and supports arithmetic operations. These results demonstrate the potential of remote vibration sensing to infer spatial layouts hidden from view.

items.title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis
items.content: arXiv:2611.25935v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. A blob twin blends an altered copy of a real frame with the frame itself, targeting blending artifacts. It needs no generator and no face-shaped mask. Together, these twins provide two complementary forensic cues that generalize to unseen manipulations. TwinDreaches a mean AUROC of 96.3%, 8.9 points above the prior state-of-the-art, with 98.1% on the blending datasets and 95.6% on the EFS datasets. Trained on twins alone, without a deepfake dataset, single models still reach 94.3% on average over three seeds. For reproducibility, the code, trained model, and training data are at: https://github.com/yermandy/TwinD
items.author: Andrii Yermakov, Jan Cech, Mario Fritz, Jiri Matas
items.summary: Shows that facial deepfake detectors trained on blending artifacts collapse on entire-face synthesis (EFS): the best prior detector achieves 96.2% mean AUROC on blending datasets but under 78.1% on EFS datasets across a 19-dataset benchmark spanning 2019-2026. TwinD trains on fakes plus reconstruction and neural-trace twins generated from real frames, closing the generalization gap without requiring EFS training data. Includes authors Mario Fritz and Jiri Matas.
items.reasoning: The generalization failure of deepfake detectors on modern whole-face synthesis is an important, quantified finding, and the twin-based training strategy is an elegant solution requiring no EFS fakes. Strong author credibility and a thorough benchmark add weight, though deepfake detection is a contested arms race.

items.title: Beyond Covers and Titles: Evidence-First Ranking for Robust Cold-Start Recommendation
items.content: arXiv:2611.26249v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Short-video platforms rank new uploads before anyone has watched them, using content towers that read a video's cover, title and frames. Existing attacks on content-aware recommenders perturb pixels or features and ignore platform re-encoding, and existing defenses train against norm-bounded perturbations that neither match real edits nor preserve recommendation quality. We show with REAP, a realizable attack through {a simulated platform channel (H.264 transcoding, rescaling, cropping and JPEG)}, that packaging edits raise a cold video by 32.0 rank-percentile points in unrelated audiences. We then observe that cold-start ranking does not need the packaging at all: a tower that sees only the video body ranks cold items best. Building on this, we propose Evidence-First Ranking (EFR), which scores cold videos from their body, admits packaging only through a support-gated residual bounded by $\gamma$, and merges cold and warm rankings by rank percentile, yielding an exact certificate against any packaging edit. On MicroLens-100K, EFR cuts the attack gain by 81% and raises cold-start Recall@100 from 0.1133 to 0.170, while keeping the merged NDCG@10 within 4% of the undefended system.
items.author: Fuyi Wang, Yuxin Cao, Yifan Liao, Renyang Liu, Lin Li, Wei Song
items.summary: This work demonstrates REAP, a realistic attack on content-aware recommender systems that survives platform channels like H.264 transcoding, cropping, and JPEG compression, raising cold videos by 32 rank-percentile points via packaging edits. It then proposes an evidence-first defense showing that ranking on the video body alone outperforms packaging-based towers and resists manipulation.
items.reasoning: Combines a realistic adversarial analysis of short-video recommender systems with an actionable, counterintuitive defense; the security-relevant findings and simulation of real platform channels strengthen impact for industry systems.

items.title: Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain
items.content: arXiv:2611.26511v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. items.title: Learning to Move from and for Manipulation Policies: Spatializing Latent Action Representations for Goal-Pose-Free Mobile Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.25366v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The success of manipulation policies is closely tied to the spatial relationship between the robot and the target object, as well as the task being performed, making the ability to adjust the robot's pose critical for successful execution. When the robot starts away from the task, such adjustments require coordinating navigation with local manipulation. Jointly training these capabilities incurs substantial computational and data costs, while navigating toward a predefined goal pose limits the flexibility needed to adapt to task-specific manipulation requirements. To address these challenges, we propose Learning to Move from and for Manipulation Policies (M4M), a framework that learns manipulation-aware mobility directly from pretrained manipulation policies. By leveraging the hidden representations of the policy's action-generating network as dense supervision, together with a limited number of manipulation execution outcomes, we learn a spatially conditioned embedding that captures task-dependent manipulation success across candidate robot poses. From the robot's current stereo observations, this representation estimates manipulation success at unvisited poses without rolling out the manipulation policy at each location. It is further integrated into navigation policy training, while a learned handoff policy decides when to transition from navigation to manipulation, enabling the robot to move and manipulate in a unified, task-aware manner. Across eight articulated-object tasks in unseen RoboCasa kitchens, M4M achieves 47.0% mean task success, compared with 26.5% for the strongest baseline and 19.2% for direct manipulation execution, and refrigerator-closing experiments show consistent improvements across four frozen manipulation policies.

items.summary: M4M learns manipulation-aware mobility directly from pretrained manipulation policies, allowing a mobile robot to position itself for successful manipulation without a predefined goal pose. items.title: Learning optimal gaits and styles for terrain-adaptive quadruped locomotion
items.content: arXiv:2611.25958v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Animals use many different gaits to locomote at different speeds across varying terrains. A longstanding question in biology and robotics is: which gait is best? This question is most often addressed from an energy-efficiency perspective on flat terrain, leaving open how the answer depends on terrain and on the criterion optimized. Here we show that gait optimality is determined jointly by terrain, performance metric, and velocity. We use deep reinforcement learning and networks of abstract oscillators, modeling spinal central pattern generators, to learn 11 quadrupedal gaits across diverse challenging terrains, together with the locomotion style (base height, foot ground clearance, foot offsets) that each requires. A second policy then selects among them to optimize a user-specified criterion such as cost of transport, base stability, or joint smoothness. Across these performance metrics and within this repertoire, every gait is optimal under at least one terrain-metric-velocity combination. The framework adapts zero-shot to gait couplings and styles never seen during training, to terrains far beyond the training distribution, and to larger quadrupeds five times the training mass. With a single additional pitch-tracking reward term, the same gait couplings also support bipedal-mode locomotion. Our method provides a general and systematic way to produce expressive locomotion and to select the gait best suited to a given terrain and criterion. Project page: https://guillaume10.github.io/terrain-gaits.

items.summary: Bellegarda and Ijspeert use deep reinforcement learning with central pattern generator-inspired oscillator networks to learn 11 quadrupedal gaits across challenging terrains, jointly optimizing locomotion style parameters. A second policy then selects gaits, showing that gait optimality depends jointly on terrain, performance metric, and velocity rather than energy efficiency alone.

items.title: PhyDEX: A Benchmark for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language-Action Models via Dynamic Extrinsic Dexterity
items.content: arXiv:2611.26565v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper--object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3\%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.

This fills a real gap, since most VLA benchmarks focus only on gripper-object contact.

items.title: Towards embedded evaluations for AI monitoring
items.content:
## Executive summary

This year we observed multiple rogue agent incidents. AI monitors, often built from the developers' own internal models, are now the main oversight of internally deployed agents. Embedded evaluations address this gap: independent evaluators work inside the developer and test its safety claims. Our first pilot towards an embedded evaluation was announced with OpenAI. 

This is the third post in a series. Principles for Embedded Evaluations describes our claim-based approach to embedded evaluations. Towards embedded evaluations for scheming propensities details the claims across the deployment stages. This post applies them to AI monitoring, i.e. the system that detects model misbehaviour during internal deployment. We explicitly do not discuss containment mechanisms in this post, like sandboxes or blocking interventions, which could help constrain damage from an incident. Rather, we focus on whether an agent subverting a monitor would be noticed and the incident disclosed appropriately.

Concretely, we propose the following six monitoring detection claims:

- Claim 1 (coverage): Monitors are deployed across all internal deployment contexts.
- Claim 2 (capability): If rogue internal deployment (RID) were to occur, monitors would detect it.
- Claim 3 (trust): The monitors are trusted.
- Claim 4 (disclosure): Any detected incidents are disclosed appropriately.
- Claim 5 (past deployments): No RID was attempted and missed so far.
- Claim 6 (future deployments): Monitoring will be adequate for the next internal deployment.

In the conclusion, we describe how these claims could in the future be extended to include containment.

## Introduction. Why do we need embedded evaluations for AI monitoring?...

items.title: SiliconGym: A Versatile Reinforcement Learning Environment for Agentic EDA
items.content: arXiv:2611.25658v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with electronic design automation (EDA) feedback is advancing large language models for hardware design and verification. Extending these gains to hardware-engineering agents requires environments that span tasks, preserve state across tool calls, and support large hierarchies alongside parallel rollouts. We present SiliconGym, the first versatile, cross-task and cross-toolchain RL environment for hardware design and verification. By decoupling versioned workspaces, budgeted execution, and acceptance-gated scoring, SiliconGym scales from module-level RTL, testbench, and PPA tasks to multi-round repository repair and full-hierarchy SoC flows. Streaming dispatch overlaps tool checks with generation, finishing a 256-answer RL batch 21.9% faster than native ChipSeek. Using interchangeable open-source and commercial backends, we show that open-source-trained functional correctness transfers cleanly to commercial simulation, while paired netlist evaluation reveals when open-source PPA gains survive commercial synthesis.
items.author: Hejia Zhang, Sheng Lu, Yitong Ma, Zhongming Yu, Zhijing Wu, Wentao Ni, Chia-Tung Ho, Jishen Zhao

This enables training agentic LLMs for EDA workflows.

Practical importance for agentic EDA is high, though it is an environment contribution rather than a new algorithmic result.

items.title: Duopra: From Full-Duplex Conversation to Full-Duplex Agency
items.content: arXiv:2611.25773v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Full-duplex interaction models exhibit strong conversational agency, enabling natural, low-latency turn-taking, backchannels, and interruptions. However, completing tasks further requires task agency: timely tool invocation and argument revision following user corrections. Frontend-backend agents separate initiation from execution: the frontend decides whether and what to request, while the backend determines how. Execution can be offloaded, but unsent requests cannot be executed, and incomplete ones can misdirect the backend. On Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (FDB v3), most failures of Realtime-Venus-Audio + Harness in our streaming pipeline occur before a domain tool executes. We introduce Duopra, a full-duplex interaction model that learns task execution alongside conversational control. Duopra treats the backend as a tool, accepting a self-contained natural-language request. Direct calls and backend delegation share an action interface and requirements for faithful initiation and correct execution. Its three-stage training combines protocol SFT, full-duplex RL rewarding timely and complete execution, and projector-only repair of talker conditioning after thinker updates. With the same backend, Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7%; Duopra achieves 47.7% calling tools directly (26.0% after SFT) and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend. It improves three FDB v1.0 takeover rates over the base model. These results show that task agency can coexist with key conversational agency.
items.author: Chiyu Chen, Pengzhou Cheng, Yuezhao Ma, Xiaocheng Li, Can Liu, Haonan Hu, Yao Yao, Yifei Yang, Yijie Lu, Taolei Wang, Yansi Li, Muhuan Wu, Chenglu Sun, Gongshen Liu, Zhuosheng Zhang

The paper diagnoses that most failures in a streaming pipeline occur before any domain tool executes, and trains the model to learn task execution within the full-duplex interaction paradigm.
items.reasoning: Extends an active research frontier (real-time full-duplex voice agents) from conversation to tool use, with a new benchmark usage (FDB v3) and a systems-level frontend/backend decomposition that is architecturally interesting. Novelty is good, though author credibility and external validation are still limited to a single benchmark.

items.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
items.content: arXiv:2611.24969v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

items.summary: Introduces PRKV, a training-free KV cache eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance via Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs, propagating importance beyond recency or instantaneous attention. It matches established eviction baselines on long-context, retrieval, and chain-of-thought tasks even at up to 90% compression, with low overhead. Addresses the central memory bottleneck of long-context LLM inference.

items.title: MATE: Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution for Safe and Efficient Mobile Control
items.content: arXiv:2611.25526v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Mobile agents on personal smartphones can affect private data, payments, settings, and the foreground screen. We present MATE (Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution), an execution-layer system that controls the boundary between agent action proposals and device effects without modifying the underlying model. MATE represents each UI primitive as a structured action record that combines the instruction, target app, screen context, primitive, and action fields. Runtime Guardrail (RG) maps this record to an allow, block, or user-approval decision; Predefined Task Routing (PTR) serves recurring requests through verified routes with post-execution screen checks; and a floating interface keeps execution in a compact overlay. On MobileSafetyBench, MATE raises high-risk blocking from 29.7% to 97.0% under GPT-4o. On AndroidWorld, it reduces LLM calls by up to 6x and raises recurring-use task success to 95.7%.

It improves safety and efficiency on MobileSafetyBench for agents operating on personal smartphones.

items.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.25760v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer--agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, \NaturalPositiveShare{}\% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

items.title: {\phi}TD: Distributional Reinforcement Learning using Characteristic Functions
items.content: arXiv:2611.25208v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Distributional Reinforcement Learning methods aim to learn the entire distribution of returns, yet current algorithmic approaches are limited to a narrow class of distributions. We propose $\varphi$TD, a method to overcome this limitation by computing the loss in the frequency domain. We demonstrate that this further unifies quantile and categorical approaches to distributional RL, and enables the learning of distributions that were previously impossible to capture, such as mixtures of continuous distributions. We empirically study $\varphi$TD, across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments and demonstrate that the flexibility obtained from wider parametric families can lead to improved performance.

items.summary: PhiTD computes distributional RL losses in the frequency domain via characteristic functions, unifying quantile and categorical approaches and enabling learning of previously uncapturable return distributions such as mixtures of continuous distributions. Empirical results span synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments, showing performance gains from richer parametric families.
items.reasoning: A conceptually elegant contribution to distributional RL theory with demonstrated large-scale empirical results; frequency-domain losses are a fresh angle, though adoption depends on practical stability in mainstream RL pipelines.

items.title: DTS: Delta-Based Tile Scoring for Efficient Long-Context Sparse Attention
items.content: arXiv:2611.25938v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.

items.title: RL Can Only Reinforce What It Sees Succeed
items.content: arXiv:2611.26084v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player, so that the prior and the right answer are exact. Base models hedge as their corpus did, and RL turns that hedging into decisions, in whichever direction the reward favours. But RL can only reinforce what it sees succeed. When the right action is rare, each run either learns it everywhere or not at all, and which runs take off is predicted before training by one count: the expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins. About 35 such groups give even odds. The count holds for new and repeated problems and for groups of 4 to 256 attempts, and across learning rates, optimizers, GRPO variants and model sizes from 1.3M to 85M parameters, which move the threshold but not what is counted.
items.author: Ruben Sanchez-Corcuera, Unai Zulaika, Aritz Bilbao-Jayo, Miguel Fernandez-de-Retana
items.summary: Studies outcome-reward RL in a fully controlled puzzle world where small language models are trained from scratch on games from a known Bayesian player, showing RL converts pre-training hedging into reward-favored decisions but cannot reinforce actions that are never observed to succeed. Run-level success is predicted by the expected number of attempt groups containing the correct action.
items.reasoning: Clean, falsifiable experimental design yielding an interpretable predictor of RL take-off and a crisp statement about exploration limits of outcome-reward RL on language models. The controlled setting limits direct transfer to frontier-scale training but the insight is broadly relevant to RLVR-style methods.

items.title: From Benchmarks to the Bench: Preference, Correspondence and Selectivity in Bidirectional Drug-Target Screening
items.content: arXiv:2611.26369v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Identifying active molecules for known targets and potential targets for existing drugs is central to drug discovery and repurposing. Drug-target interaction (DTI) models can rank vast numbers of drug-target pairs, but limited experimental capacity restricts testing to a small number of candidates. We compared the bidirectional recommendations of 13 released systems across 711 molecular structures of FDA-approved drugs and 614 human proteins. For the same target or drug, pairs of models produced completely disjoint Top-10 molecule and protein lists in 77.8% and 70.1% of comparisons, respectively. Even where recommendations overlapped, agreement between some systems largely reflected recurring preferences for the same candidates. Published inhibition measurements for 79 molecules and 65 kinases revealed that some systems enriched active candidates, yet their hit yields changed little when recommendations were matched to different drugs or targets, whereas other systems lost substantially more hits. Some of the former systems also rarely ranked both molecules and kinases correctly when two drugs favoured different kinases. We further retrained the same architecture on the same data, with the training objective fixed and random seeds varied. Despite similar test performance, mean pairwise Top-10 overlap on a separate screening catalogue was about two candidates. Our study moves DTI model evaluation beyond benchmark performance to assess whether model predictions can guide meaningful experimental decisions in drug discovery and target identification.

Rigorous comparative design at meaningful scale; the score reflects high applied relevance for AI in drug discovery, though the work is diagnostic rather than offering a fix.

items.title: Physical Laws without Physics Loss? Probing Learned Dynamics in Video World Models through Forced Response
items.content: arXiv:2611.25626v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Do video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss, or merely imitate motion? Overall motion and appearance scores cannot settle it. We investigate this through nonlinear forced response: an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. We introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapt six image-to-video backbones to predict this motion using only the flow-matching loss. Wan predicts motion accurately and generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes. Counterfactual tests suggest capabilities beyond replaying training videos. But what laws have they learned? We design three tiers of tests using Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry. All six reproduce the linear response, including resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics, including nonlinear softening. Remarkably, softening is barely present in training: only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts. Yet learned dynamics may fail to appear when state estimation or propagation goes wrong. We turn these tests and findings into strategies to improve video training and generation.

Wan-based models predict motion accurately and generalize to unseen excitations, and tiered tests based on Taylor expansions of dynamics reveal that all six backbones reproduce linear responses including resonance, but diverge at higher-order regimes.
items.reasoning: A well-designed scientific evaluation of a central question about world models, with rigorous tiered testing methodology and counterfactual analyses. Timely given the rapid growth of video world models, and the finding that models capture linear dynamics but not higher-order laws is a meaningful insight, though reliant on a limited excitation paradigm.

items.title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
items.content: arXiv:2611.26627v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

This suggests RL post-training in diffusion models works primarily via representational shifting rather than complex input-dependent computation.

items.title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
items.content: arXiv:2611.25179v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.

items.title: Streaming-AAA: Streaming AAA Game Video Generation at High Resolution, High Frame Rate, and Low Latency
items.content: arXiv:2611.26040v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.

This pushes interactive game video generation close to practical gameplay requirements.

items.title: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.26211v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement.
