items.title: Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.25891v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand- engineered. We present Meta-RTL, an EDA-grounded framework that evolves RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop while keeping the optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL* reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70% of them. Without further evolution, Meta-RTL* transfers to 10 unseen IC-RTL designs, reducing aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and total synthesized area by 12.6%. We further characterize three search mechanisms in the evolved harness and assess their contributions through ablations and a case study.
items.author: Xinzhuang Xiong, Yonghao Wang, Shengyao Sun, Chengxi Li, Evangeline Young
items.summary: Meta-RTL uses LLM-driven evolution of agent harnesses for hardware RTL optimization with EDA feedback, evolving the search procedure itself while keeping the model, EDA flow, and budgets fixed. Compared to Dr. RTL, the evolved Meta-RTL* cuts aggregate WNS/TNS violations substantially on development designs and transfers to unseen designs with double-digit improvements plus area reductions.

Good transfer evidence to unseen designs; impact confined mainly to the chip-design/agents niche, but the harness-evolution approach has broader implications.

items.title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
items.content: arXiv:2611.25597v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

items.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark
items.content: arXiv:2611.25252v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.

items.title: Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration: Bootstrapping Generative Auto-bidding from Narrow Support
items.content: arXiv:2611.26060v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Auto-bidding is a core algorithmic component in online advertising auctions. In practical cold-start settings, iterative training is commonly used to compensate for low-quality, narrowly supported historical data. Unfortunately, in iterative training, representative diffusion-based AI-Generated Bidding (AIGB) methods fail to sustain extrapolation beyond the narrow data support and stagnate at a suboptimal level. In this paper, we theoretically attribute this stagnation to Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) collapse: the weak radial return signal is overwhelmed by a curvature-induced penalty. To break this stagnation, we propose \textbf{Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration (ISGE)}, which introduces a guidance handoff: as the return signal collapses, scarcity subsequently takes over as an exploratory signal to elevate the SNR above a critical threshold. Specifically, ISGE iteratively alternates between a \emph{Judger} that assigns scarcity scores to trajectories and an \emph{Explorer} that performs guided generation of high-scarcity and high-return trajectories, thereby bootstrapping from the narrow support with such self-generated trajectories. Extensive experiments on the industrial AuctionNet benchmark demonstrate that ISGE, starting from cold-start datasets, effectively surpasses the performance of the Full-Dataset baseline within three iterations. Code is available at https://github.com/alimama-tech/ISGE

items.title: Sequential Anytime Valid Tests for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment
items.content: arXiv:2611.26413v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-N (BoN), improve language model outputs by generating multiple candidates per prompt and selecting among them using a reward model. Much of this cost is wasted: a fixed budget is applied to every prompt, although the computation required by prompts varies widely. Adaptive methods halt once sampled answers appear settled, but their thresholds are tuned heuristics with no statistical control over early-stopping errors. We instead seek an anytime-valid stopping rule that takes an error tolerance $\alpha$ as input and halts only once an answer is certified to hold a majority ($\theta_a > 1/2$) under the generator's distribution. We aggregate candidates by final answer with a reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) score and treat stopping as a sequential test over the resulting clusters. Applying Wald's sequential probability ratio test to these clusters yields SPRT-RWSC, which performs well empirically, but its guarantee fails because the leading answer shifts during sampling, and the run is continuously monitored. Our main contribution, e-RWSC, replaces Wald's test with a betting supermartingale (an e-process) for every answer the policy produces, bounding the probability of ever certifying a non-dominant answer by $\alpha$, uniformly over time and across all answers. The RWSC scores drive the bets, so they affect only how quickly a dominant answer $a^\star$ is certified, not validity; certification takes $O(\log(1/\alpha)/d_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta_{a^\star}\|1/2))$ samples. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward models confirm the predicted $1/d_{\mathrm{KL}}$ scaling of cost and show that accuracy improves over baselines at substantially lower token cost.

items.title: Accord: Universal Online Metric Localization and Dense Mapping from one Camera and an IMU
items.content: arXiv:2611.25279v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem. What is essential is the multi-view agreement (Accord), which is considered in SLAM as a source of geometric self-consistency. Accord anchors each keyframe window to metric 3D points triangulated from the filter poses, then exploits bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to estimate and correct per-image scale errors while preserving the metric scale established by the anchors. Context keyframes further improve depth prediction, and the resulting submaps are fused in a factor graph. We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset. With nothing tuned per dataset/setup and every map aligned only by Accord's own trajectory, Accord achieves consistently best/second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform. Accord is open-source along with the phone-rig dataset for the benefit of the research community

items.title: CANDOR: Contrastive Self-Denoising Rewards for Label-Free Text-to-Image Post-Training
items.content: arXiv:2611.25457v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Post-training text-to-image generators with reinforcement learning usually relies on external reward models that need annotated preferences or auxiliary evaluators and are prone to reward hacking. We show that the generator's own denoising accuracy, used by a recent intrinsic reward, is a poor proxy for prompt fidelity. Within a same-prompt group, this absolute self-confidence is dominated by image complexity and ranks correct samples above incorrect ones near chance. We introduce CANDOR (Contrastive Alignment from Null-referenced Denoising lOg-Ratio), the log-ratio of unconditional to conditional denoising errors under shared noise probes, which measures how much the prompt helps the model denoise its own sample. It cancels prompt-independent difficulty that scales both errors and ranks the better of two same-prompt samples higher in 60% and 63% of pairs on compositional generation and text rendering. As the only Flow-GRPO reward for a flow-matching model, CANDOR improves text rendering, aesthetic and human-preference scores over the base model and a prior absolute self-confidence reward, with text-rendering and preference gains that stronger classifier-free guidance does not reproduce. On public Flow-GRPO adapters trained on external rewards, CANDOR further raises PickScore and ImageReward, so it can complement those rewards. Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/candor.

items.title: MultiBinder: Preventing Multi-Subject Identity Leakage in Personalized Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.26164v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Personalized video generation faces a significant scalability challenge: as the number of custom subjects increases, existing methods suffer from severe identity leakage and semantic entanglement, resulting in videos with blended attributes and incoherent narratives. We identify that this stems from a lack of explicit binding between textual entity phrases and their corresponding visual patterns prior to fusion in diffusion models. To address this, we propose MultiBinder, a novel framework built on a ``bind-then-narrate'' paradigm. Our approach introduces a two-stage conditioning process before video diffusion. First, Cross-modal Entity Binding devises an entity-aware Q-Former to extract identity-centric features from each subject's reference image and tightly align them with its unique entity phrase, yielding disentangled ``identity tokens.'' Second, a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) acts as a ``narrative director'' in the Narrative-Aware Subject Arrangement stage, capturing the action of each subject from the text prompt and synthesizes contextualized subject features that encapsulate ``who is doing what'' and preserve role-specific distinctions. These features are then injected into a video diffusion model via dedicated conditioning pathways, ensuring precise attribute allocation. Extensive experiments on both general and newly curated multi-subject benchmarks show that MultiBinder significantly outperforms existing methods in multi-subject identity fidelity.

items.reasoning: Solves a real scalability pain point in personalized generative video with a well-motivated binding mechanism; meaningful contribution to generative modeling, but within a crowded subfield of subject-driven generation.

items.title: CauSyncVLA: Causal Latent World Modeling for Asynchronous Robot Control
items.content: arXiv:2611.25667v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies must react while visual inference is still running. Overlapping computation and execution reduces waiting, yet leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected. We present CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller that aligns perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction with actual robot execution. Rather than forecasting pixels or physical states, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history, supervised through action-sensitive distillation to retain the frozen expert's control response. Conditioned on this updated memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training. On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA reaches 93.8% success at 5.04$\times$ inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness.

Predictive Flow Warm-Starting then aligns unexecuted action chunks with the updated memory.

items.title: GraF-VTA: Neuro-Symbolic Trajectory Generation from Vision and Temporal Logic via Graph-Based Fusion
items.content: arXiv:2611.25589v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robotic planning from visual observations and signal temporal logic (STL) requires grounding task requirements in scene evidence while adapting plans to execution feedback. We present GraF-VTA, a graph-based framework that extends Vision-TL-Action with structured task representations, causal observation history, and closed-loop trajectory generation. Bidirectional cross-attention fuses STL syntax tokens with visual features, while an optional frozen automaton embedding supplies complementary untimed task structure. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations and compresses older frames to provide recent execution context. Conditioned on these features and robot state, a flow-matching model generates plans whose action prefixes are executed before replanning from refreshed observations. Across five simulation environments, the single-graph configuration achieves higher open-loop Success@$K$ than TeLoGraF and Vision-TL-Action on four environments at the reported budgets $K\geq16$. On Panda, matched-update ablations increase Success@256 from 53.91\% without observation history to 62.50\% with pyramid memory. In closed-loop Dubins evaluation, it reaches 64.06\% Success@1024, compared with 12.50\% for adapted S-MSP and 27.34\% for adapted Logic-VLA. These results support combining structured visual conditioning with observation history and replanning to improve coverage of STL-satisfying trajectories.

It grounds formal task requirements in scene evidence while adapting to feedback.

items.title: A Verifier from the Past: Test-Time Compute for Time Series Foundation Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25171v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.
items.author: Arjun Choudhry, Aditya Narayanan, Raghav Mallampalli, Po-han Li, Sai Shankar Narasimhan, Raimi Shah, B. Aditya Prakash, Shubhankar Agarwal
items.summary: This paper introduces BGAA (Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging), a test-time compute algorithm adapted for time series foundation models. The key insight is that standard test-time compute verification cannot work directly for forecasting since a causal forecaster cannot score candidates using future information; instead, BGAA builds a verifier from the series' own history via rolling-origin backtests, filters out context transformations that underperform the unmodified context, and averages the predictive distributions of surviving candidates. The approach reportedly improves performance across all tested TSFM benchmarks.
items.reasoning: The paper addresses a genuine conceptual gap: transplanting test-time compute techniques from language models to time series forecasting requires a causal verifier design, which is a novel and principled contribution. Its broad empirical gains across benchmarks strengthen the result. However, it is a domain-specific technique for a smaller research area rather than a frontier-model advance, and the abstract suggests incremental gains on existing models, so impact is likely confined to the time series forecasting community.

The key insight is that standard test-time compute verification cannot work directly for forecasting since a causal forecaster cannot score candidates using future information; instead, BGAA builds a verifier from the series' own history via rolling-origin backtests, filters out context transformations that underperform the unmodified context, and averages the predictive distributions of surviving candidates. The approach reportedly improves performance across all tested TSFM benchmarks.

A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.

items.title: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
items.content: arXiv:2611.25357v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.

items.title: Toward a Science of AI Agent Societies
items.content: arXiv:2611.25404v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI agents are rapidly evolving from isolated personal assistants into networked actors that interact with one another at scale. We envision the emergence of AI agent societies, with their own social and economic dynamics, as a new research frontier. We argue that AI agent societies should be studied as a distinct object of inquiry: neither simply larger collections of individual agents nor merely simulations of human society. To formalize this perspective, we propose four core properties that a valid AI agent society should satisfy: individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity. Building on this framework, we identify four classes of societal behaviors worth studying in AI agent societies: economic behaviors, behaviors under conflict-of-interest, unsafe and unethical behaviors, and system-level behaviors. We then outline key technical challenges--including property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation--and argue that progress on these challenges could enable scientifically informative and practically useful models of AI agent societies. Finally, we revisit existing multi-agent systems through the lens of the proposed core properties, show that they instantiate only subsets of them, and discuss implications for platform design, evaluation, and governance.

items.title: How Feedback-Free Self-Evolution Reshapes Agent Skills: A Systematic Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.25534v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Agent skills are documents in which experts write down procedural knowledge, and models increasingly maintain them by rewriting them without feedback. Such rewriting could adapt a skill to the model that uses it or erode the expert knowledge that makes it useful, yet how skills evolve under this feedback-free self-evolution has not been studied. We let models rewrite expert skills round after round without any task, run or judgment and run agents built on the same models with the rewritten skills. Our experiments show that the skills lose value rather than improve, as every model we test performs worse with them on every benchmark, by 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. Sampling each model's prior with skills it writes from the topic alone, we find that rewriting pulls skills toward this prior and gives up first the knowledge outside it. Putting this knowledge back recovers much of the lost pass rate, so an expert's skill is valuable largely for what the model does not write on its own. Building on this insight, SkillDiff marks this knowledge in place and raises the pass rate on SkillsBench by 4.8 points on average without feedback or any change to the skill's text. Project repository: https://github.com/LitaoGuo/How-Self-Evolution-Reshapes-Skills.
items.author: Litao Guo, Man Chen, Xinli Xu, Jinsong Zhou, Zixin Zhang, Ying-Cong Chen
items.summary: This systematic study examines what happens when LLM agents rewrite expert-written skill documents repeatedly without any task feedback or judgment. The surprising finding is negative: skills degrade rather than improve, with every tested model performing worse using rewritten skills, dropping about 15 points on average on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. This cautions against unsupervised self-evolution of agent procedural knowledge.
items.reasoning: Rigorous negative-result study on an emerging practice (feedback-free skill rewriting by agents); the systematic, multi-model benchmarking and clear degradation finding are valuable for the agent self-improvement literature. Novelty is solid, though the conclusion may be anticipated by model-collapse intuitions.

items.title: Decoupled Knowledge Retrieval and Compact Memory Enable Reliable Lifelong Model Editing
items.content: arXiv:2611.25861v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Lifelong model editing requires continuously incorporating new facts into deployed large language models (LLMs) without expensive retraining or compromising existing capabilities. Memory-based editors offer an appealing solution by keeping the base parameters untouched, yet their practical use is hindered by linearly growing storage requirements and deteriorating retrieval performance as edits accumulate. To tackle these problems, we introduce BiSpace, a lifelong model editing framework that decouples memory retrieval from knowledge injection across two distinct representation spaces. BiSpace routes queries and identifies relevant edits in an external semantic space, while injecting the corresponding knowledge into the internal representation space of the LLM through sparse and storage-efficient updates. Extensive experiments show that BiSpace shrinks each entry's storage to only about 10.2% of the original and shows strong resilience to long edit sequences of up to 16K edits. On a more challenging benchmark, BiSpace further improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods. These results advance memory-based editing toward reliable long-term model maintenance at scale.

items.title: System-One RSI: Building Muscle Memory for Interactive Agents through Guided Practice
items.content: arXiv:2611.26007v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reasoning models provide strong multimodal task understanding but struggle with sub-second control because deliberation increases decision latency. Fast decision models can meet the response window, yet prompting and few-shot examples do not readily provide the fine-grained experience required by a new task. Inspired by coached motor learning, this paper presents System-One Recursive Self-Improvement (System-One RSI), which couples two loops. The high-frequency online inner loop is an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (OODA) cycle: a decision model maps each visual observation and task question to structured judgments, and a decision tree converts them into timed actions without invoking a reasoning model. The offline outer loop is a recursive improvement cycle carried out by a team of reasoning agents. The team revises the decision-model prompt and decision tree, captures interaction records, derives supervision from those records, and trains or deploys updated model parameters. The improved system then returns to the environment and generates the experience for the next round, consolidating learned distinctions as external muscle memory. The framework operates with a small number of real episodes, without expert demonstrations, environment modification, sandboxing, or parallel simulation. Experiments in Snake, Zenless Zone Zero, and Black Myth: Wukong use a 27B decision model. Mean Snake score increases from 1.30 to 7.35. In an evaluated scenario of Zenless Zone Zero, median completion time decreases by 8.4%. In an evaluated combat scenario of Black Myth: Wukong, the evasive policy achieves 11 times the mean survival time of a stationary reference, while the offensive policy win rate rises from 0% to 66.7% across the evaluated configurations.
items.author: Qingxu Fu, Xuanfa Jin, Ziqian Chen, Zhaoyang Liu, Bolin Ding
items.summary: System-One RSI couples a fast OODA-loop decision model that converts visual judgments into sub-second timed actions without invoking a reasoning model, with an offline recursive-improvement loop inspired by coached motor learning that distills reasoning-model competence into the fast policy. It addresses the latency problem where deliberative models miss sub-second control windows in interactive tasks.
items.reasoning: Interesting two-loop architecture tackling the real latency-capability trade-off in interactive agents, with an appealing learning analogy. The recursive self-improvement framing is somewhat inflated relative to what appears to be distillation-plus-practice; empirical strength on real interactive tasks will determine impact.

items.title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research
items.content: arXiv:2611.26171v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in the FrontierOR benchmark's one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi, with an objective within 1% of Gurobi's and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances. The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the benchmark's 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark, with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software, within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.

Baseline results show the strongest model matches Gurobi within 1% on only 39% of large instances, highlighting a substantial open gap in agentic algorithm design.

items.title: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure
items.content: arXiv:2611.24970v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in hiring pipelines is growing, yet existing evaluations generally overlook their compliance with legal rules. To fill this gap, we introduce HireWatch, an evaluation that assesses whether LLMs comply with U.S. laws that govern the questions that job candidates may be asked. We construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, whose legal classification is based on U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. We instruct LLMs to select questions from this bank in preparing for job interviews, across a set of various occupations and contexts, and report the fraction of unlawful questions that LLMs select. Evaluation of 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across ~100,000 trials under different types of contextual pressure reveals that LLMs' legal compliance is brittle. While LLMs generally avoid selecting unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher pressure. Explicit prompts to comply with law can improve compliance rates, but do not altogether eliminate legal violations. We publicly release our code and data at https://github.com/hnghiem-nlp/hirewatch_repo.

It tests 18 closed and open-weight models across roughly 100,000 trials in varied occupational contexts, measuring selection of unlawful questions. Targets a concrete legal-compliance gap in LLM hiring deployments.

items.title: VG-Steer: Visual-Geometric Policy Steering from In-Context Aligned Abstractions
items.content: arXiv:2611.25199v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/
items.author: Arthur Bucker, Pramod Anantharam, Jonathan Francis, Jean Oh
items.summary: VG-Steer corrects frozen robot policies at inference time for out-of-distribution settings by grounding corrections in explicit visual-geometric abstractions rather than signals learned implicitly from scarce robotic data. This avoids inheriting the same distribution shifts that break the underlying policy while supporting fine-grained, task-relevant motion needed for manipulation. It addresses a key bottleneck for generalist robots: adapting with limited real-world data.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real and widely acknowledged limitation of end-to-end robot policies with a sensible test-time adaptation design; the explicit-geometry grounding is a promising direction, though results breadth and baselines are not fully visible in the abstract.

items.title: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters
items.content: arXiv:2611.25235v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.
items.author: Sanidhya Vijayvargiya, Rahul Lokesh
items.summary: This paper argues that parametric memory in LLMs should not mirror continual learning's goal of indefinite retention, but instead manage a knowledge lifecycle: retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and letting transient information fade. The proposed system combines a memory substrate for storage and forgetting with a learned policy governing it. This reframes memory editing and personalization as lifecycle management rather than pure retention.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.25235v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.

items.title: FPGA-GEN: Target-Aware RTL Generation via HLS
items.content: arXiv:2611.25351v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Successful C/C++ compilation does not guarantee correct or efficient FPGA hardware after high-level synthesis (HLS). FPGA-GEN is an agentic HLS-C generation workflow that encodes specification, readiness, selection, repair, and admission rules in explicit task contracts and bounded tool-feedback loops for candidate-level decisions. On HLS-Eval, five shared-context outputs per task yield 407/425 (95.8%) public-testbench passes. In a cumulative conversion campaign, FPGA-GEN admits 104/107 (97.2%) HLS-LeVeri designs under held-out co-simulation, Vivado synthesis/fit, and same-RTL evidence. In focused TensorCore screening, selected candidate 3 reports 73.7% fewer CSynth cycles and 14.6% fewer LUTs than generated/composed C0, with 26.7% more DSPs, and passes development CoSim.

items.title: FG-GraphBench: Benchmarking and Enhancing Fine-Grained Visual Understanding with Multimodal Scene Graphs
items.content: arXiv:2611.25408v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to recognize small visual entities and understand their relationships. Scene graphs offer a natural way to represent this information, organizing visual entities as nodes and their relationships as edges. However, we identify two challenges: existing scene graph benchmarks provide insufficient coverage of fine-grained entities and the relationships among them, and existing methods for fine-grained visual understanding have yet to effectively leverage such graph-structured information in MLLMs. To address these challenges, we introduce Fine-Grained Multimodal Scene Graph Benchmark (FG-GraphBench) and FiGRA. FG-GraphBench is a benchmark comprising three complementary tasks: fine-grained visual question answering (FG-QA), image captioning (FG-Caption), and image description generation (FG-Description). We develop a two-stage construction pipeline that discovers and grounds fine-grained entities and establishes their relations to construct the fine-grained multimodal scene graphs (MSGs) in FG-GraphBench. Building on these MSGs, we propose FiGRA, a Fine-grained Graph Representation Augmentation method for MLLMs. FiGRA adopts a two-stage training strategy. It encodes multimodal entity and relation features as continuous graph tokens, and integrates them into the MLLM. Experiments show that FiGRA significantly outperforms strong baselines across three tasks of FG-GraphBench. Further analyses confirm the effectiveness of FG-GraphBench and highlight the importance of preserving fine-grained entity and relation information for visual understanding.

items.title: From Reliance to Overreliance: Taxonomizing and Detecting Relational Risks in AI Companionship
items.content: arXiv:2611.25734v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Companion AIs are increasingly used for emotional support, yet distinguishing meaningful engagement from harmful reliance remains difficult. We introduce the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR), which operationalizes users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately identifies evidence of relational harm (RH), enabling empirical examination of when reliance behaviors co-occur with adverse consequences. Using naturalistic Character.AI and Replika conversations from 110 adults, we found EO-related behaviors in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations, while observable relational harms appeared in 10.5%. Although EO did not necessarily lead to harm, recurring patterns often co-occurred with harmful outcomes, suggesting value as risk indicators. Open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration. Qualitative analysis revealed expectations of care, repeated support seeking, dependency, distress, and reduced confidence in personal judgment. We argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to patterns and trajectories of EO-related behavior.

items.title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management
items.content: arXiv:2611.25840v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.

items.title: ChronoPatch: Black-Box Energy-Latency Attacks on Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.26117v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as generative inference services, where autoregressive decoding makes response length a key determinant of latency and computational cost. This creates an availability risk: adversarial visual inputs can prolong generation and increase serving overhead. Existing energy-latency attacks typically rely on gradients, logits, or token-level feedback, leaving open whether such risks persist when an attacker observes only the final response. We present ChronoPatch, a black-box attack that induces prolonged VLM generation requiring only the final response. It discovers visual delay anchors through response-length-guided evolutionary search, then minimizes perturbation magnitude through subspace-calibrated decision-based optimization. Across four open-source VLMs, ChronoPatch increases inference latency by 47.86%--293.34% and GPU energy consumption by 41.44%--249.70% under a 5% spatial budget. It also induces more repetitive outputs, as reflected by increased n-gram repetition ratios. On three commercial VLM APIs, ChronoPatch increases response length by 37.6%--81.5% and client-observed latency by 1.82x--2.29x under query budgets of 500 per API. These results reveal a generation-based availability risk that persists under final-response-only access and motivate generation-aware safeguards for deployed generative AI services.

items.title: Multi-institutional grading of Barrett's esophagus dysplasia without stain normalization using a pathology foundation model and multiple instance learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.26562v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Barrett's esophagus dysplasia grading suffers substantial inter-observer variability, particularly for low-grade dysplasia, complicating clinical decision-making. We conducted a retrospective multi-institutional diagnostic accuracy study of a foundation model-based deep learning system for dysplasia grading, using 969 H\&E-stained whole slide images from four institutions. Patch-level classifiers trained on expert annotations identified diagnostically relevant regions, followed by attribute-aware multiple instance learning for slide-level classification as non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus (NDBE), low-grade dysplasia, or high-grade dysplasia. On a held-out test set (n = 130), macro-averaged AUC was 0.96 (95\% CI 0.93--0.98). For binary dysplasia detection, sensitivity was 98\% (80/82) and specificity 81\% (39/48), with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.030 and quadratic-weighted \kap{} of 0.83 against expert consensus. No high-grade dysplasia case was misclassified as NDBE. Performance was consistent across institutions without stain normalization, indicating that stain-robust foundation-model representations may remove the site-specific preprocessing that has constrained prior systems to institution-specific deployment.

items.title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
items.content: arXiv:2611.25000v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model.   At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps.   Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.

The predictor halves accuracy error versus a no-change baseline and identifies examples whose predictions flip, reducing the cost of coefficient search in merging.

items.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
items.content: arXiv:2611.25387v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.
items.author: Xuwei Ding, Skylar Zhai, Linxin Song, Jiarui Feng, Dongqi Fu, Huajun Xi, Junnan Li, Jingcheng Liang, Jieyu Zhao, Yinglong Xia, Hong Li, Jian Kang

The benchmarks cover five spatial abilities, and each task is a programmatic generator with a checker and oracle, addressing a gap left by largely solved CAPTCHA benchmarks and spatial benchmarks that lack interactive action.
items.reasoning: The interactive CAPTCHA framing is a clever, novel evaluation paradigm that tests embodied-style spatial reasoning in MLLMs, a genuine gap in current benchmarks. However, the synthetic nature and modest scale (125 CAPTCHAs) limit real-world impact, and it is an evaluation-only contribution without new model capabilities. Academic authorship with a mix of university and industry (Meta, based on affiliation pattern of authors) collaborators lends credibility.

We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

items.title: Reinforcement-Aligned Probabilistic Weather Forecasting with Discrete Tokens
items.content: arXiv:2611.25570v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Global medium-range weather forecasting must not only generate ensembles efficiently to characterize uncertainty in future states, but also serve downstream applications such as extreme-event warnings and cross-sphere coupled simulations. We introduce WeatherCraft, a framework that unifies probabilistic generation and reinforcement learning alignment through discrete weather tokens, bringing the GPT-style pretraining--post-training paradigm to global medium-range weather forecasting. A multiscale tokenizer represents atmospheric states as a coarse-to-fine token hierarchy, while a Transformer models causal dependencies across time and scale and predicts tokens within each scale in parallel. Direct sampling generates diverse ensembles, and exact token log-probabilities enable Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to maximize downstream task rewards without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models. On the ERA5 benchmark, WeatherCraft's eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% relative to the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and, with KV caching, achieves an approximately $18\times$ inference speedup over GenCast. Direct fair-CRPS adaptation improves ensemble probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves forecasts of persistent land temperature extremes and coupled ocean heat extremes. This work establishes discrete autoregressive modeling as a general foundation for scalable, task-alignable Earth system foundation models.

items.title: Goal-Guided Reinforcement Learning via Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25742v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.

items.title: How Network Topology and Data Heterogeneity Shape Decentralized Learning: A Spectral Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2611.26104v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Network topology influences decentralized federated learning through information mixing and the relative contribution of individual nodes. While existing analyses primarily focus on spectral mixing properties, they often assume doubly stochastic aggregation, overlooking topology-dependent influence under irregular communication networks. We develop a spectral framework that separates two complementary mechanisms: the dominant eigenmode determines the consensus trajectory and node influence, while non-dominant eigenmodes govern the propagation and attenuation of disagreement. Under uniform neighborhood averaging, we show that the stationary influence is proportional to node degree plus one and derive a bound relating model disagreement to spectral mixing and gradient heterogeneity. We then investigate how these mechanisms interact with the data distribution across nodes. Experiments across regular and heterogeneous network topologies reveal nearly identical learning dynamics under IID data, while network size and connectivity affect how unevenly distributed information is learned under non-IID data. For non-IID settings, we characterize how the distribution of data across nodes shapes the relative contribution of local information to consensus dynamics.

The spectral decomposition into consensus and disagreement mechanisms is elegant and could inform topology design, but the work is incremental relative to a mature literature and impact depends on empirical follow-through.

items.title: A Statistical Framework for Training Data Auditing of Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.26264v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Training-data auditing asks whether data of interest were used to train a large language model (LLM), a question central to privacy auditing, copyright protection, and benchmark-contamination detection. These concerns are particularly relevant to the use of copyrighted books and scientific papers in pre-training, as well as synthetic text and medical question-answer records in fine-tuning. In practice, training membership signals may be concentrated in only a few passages of a long document, making it important to aggregate evidence within each document without diluting these localized signals. Beyond individual documents, auditing a target collection requires an overall assessment based on the document-level evidence. In this paper, we propose a unified statistical framework for document-level membership inference, target-collection global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. We integrate complementary chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination to construct document scores for document-level membership inference. The document scores and their calibrated p-values further enable an overall assessment of training-data collection use and the identification of suspicious documents through multiple testing. Under the stated exchangeability conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework in auditing pre-training and fine-tuning data.

items.summary: The paper develops a statistical framework for auditing whether specific data were used to train an LLM, addressing privacy auditing, copyright protection, and benchmark-contamination detection. It focuses on aggregating document-level membership evidence from localized signals concentrated in a few passages of long documents, and on collection-level assessment from document-level evidence.

items.title: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent
items.content: arXiv:2611.26584v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($\Delta d' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.

items.summary: Comparing linear probes with model answers under signal detection theory across six open-weight base and post-trained model pairs, the author finds that probes detect whether German texts are human- or AI-written well while model answers do not, often inverting ordering. Post-training lowers answer sensitivity (mean delta d-prime of -0.34) and distorts use of stated base rates, suggesting post-training changes read-out of representations rather than the representations themselves.

items.title: Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants
items.content: arXiv:2611.26009v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Conversational AI assistants are now used for personal and emotional support. Developers report improvements in how new models respond to sensitive conversations, yet users and civil society continue to raise concerns about their behaviour in real-world, repeated interactions that safety evaluations rarely capture. Often, evaluations present signs of distress clearly and in a single message, even though people may reveal their struggles gradually in otherwise ordinary conversations. We worked with three community mental health support workers to test if models provide the same level of safeguarding when cues are shared all at once or gradually over time. We designed nine scenarios in which a user shares cues related to depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse. For each scenario, the support workers established a gold standard response, ranging from signposting support to pausing the everyday task to address safeguarding. We presented five cues either together in one message or dispersed across a conversation. Across more than 7,400 conversations, we evaluated six widely used models from five developers. GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick met the support workers' standards in just 26-59% of conversations when cues were concentrated, and only 3-6% when dispersed. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 showed a smaller gap, meeting the standards in 68-97% of concentrated conversations and 59-87% of dispersed conversations. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5, fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when cues were dispersed. Safety evaluations centred on explicit, legible concerns can overstate how well safeguards protect people when signs of distress emerge gradually or indirectly through ordinary conversations. For claims of improved safety to be taken seriously, developers must design and assess safeguards around how people actually communicate.

items.summary: Working with three community mental health support workers, the authors designed nine scenarios where distress cues are shared gradually over multi-turn conversations rather than stated plainly in one message, testing whether AI assistants maintain safeguarding quality. The study addresses a gap between standard single-turn safety evaluations and real-world, repeated emotional-support interactions.

items.title: When Sounds Turn Heads: Recovering Event Timing That Audio LLMs Fail to Say
items.content: arXiv:2611.25960v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Audio LLMs can know when a queried sound occurs but fail to say it. We find a few attention heads that track the queried sound: they shift when the query changes, follow the sound when it moves, and removing or blocking them often hurts the model's timestamps. Yet the answer does not express what they track. Intervals read directly from these heads outperform the model's original answer and recover events that its timestamps miss. To bring this timing into the answer, we introduce head-guided decoding, which needs no training. It keeps the model's decision on whether the sound is present and rescores its candidate timestamps with a prior from these heads. Heads selected on development data transfer unchanged to new recordings and free-text queries, where head-guided decoding improves the timestamps of three audio LLMs, scores above their head readout on every benchmark, and, in most settings, outperforms random-head guidance. On recordings released after the models were trained, head-guided decoding raises mIoU from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56. These results suggest that poor temporal answers in audio LLMs partly reflect a failure to say rather than to hear, and that the model's own attention can close part of this gap.

items.title: Search or Scoring? Diagnosing Why Visual World-Model Planners Fail
items.content: arXiv:2611.25347v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual world models such as DINO-WM and JEPA-WM plan with an optimizer that searches for actions whose predicted outcome has the lowest cost, its distance to a goal image. A plan can thus fail in two ways: the optimizer never tries a good action that the cost would prefer (a search failure), or the cost, computed on predictions, ranks a bad action first (a scoring failure). The two need different remedies, more search or a better model, but a planner does not record which one occurred. We tell them apart by executing the optimizer's candidates, scoring a known solution with the planner's own cost, and comparing costs on predicted and real outcomes. An error model explains when each arises and so how to use retrieved demonstration windows (DemoProp): start the search from them (a warm start) when prediction errors are small, and average them without the model when large errors make the optimizer pick overrated actions. Across four simulated environments and three world models, on short tasks whose goals the planner can represent, PushT and Wall fail mostly by search, while Metaworld and RoboCasa fail by scoring because the cost, sound on real outcomes (AUROC 0.94 on Metaworld), is at chance on predictions (0.54). The diagnosis tells which remedy pays off: a four times larger search lowers the real-outcome cost only where failures come from search (clearly for DINO-WM), and where they come from scoring, averaging the windows without the model solves 127 of 168 new Metaworld tasks, against at most 87 when the model chooses among them. Within PushT, degrading only the model flips which use is better, and our rule, frozen in advance, follows the flip and solves 678 of 960 new episodes, against 530 for the best fixed use.
items.author: Haoxuan Jia, Yang Liu, Shang Luo, Chenhao Wu, Zixiang Ni, Yingguang Yang, Feng Zhang, Chongyang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Kefu Xu, Congjing Ran, Jifeng Zhu, Bin Chong
items.summary: This paper introduces a diagnostic framework for visual world-model planners like DINO-WM and JEPA-WM that distinguishes between search failures, where the optimizer never proposes a good action, and scoring failures, where the cost function ranks a bad action first. By executing candidate actions and comparing costs on predicted versus real outcomes, the method identifies which failure mode occurred, enabling targeted fixes such as more search or a better model.
items.reasoning: Provides a clean conceptual decomposition of planner failure modes in visual world models, which is directly relevant to embodied AI and model-based planning. The diagnostic methodology is practical, though the scope is limited to existing WM architectures.

items.title: Query-Aware vs. Query-Agnostic Training-Free Video Token Pruning in Multimodal LLMs
items.content: arXiv:2611.25537v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video Large Language Models process large numbers of visual tokens, making token pruning important for efficient inference. Training-free pruning methods differ in whether and how they use the user query, and the value of query conditioning remains unclear. We present a controlled study of training-free, pre-LLM video token selection. Using a shared Qwen-3-VL backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings, we compare 21 pruning principles spanning query-agnostic, shallow query-conditioned, structured query-conditioned, and holistic strategies. To instantiate the last two categories, we introduce Structured Query Pruning, which decomposes the question into semantic anchors, and a Pareto variant, which combines anchor relevance with query-agnostic visual diversity. Across Video-MME, MVBench, and LongVideoBench, relevance computed from the raw question embedding is unreliable (8--16 points below the best methods), whereas anchors derived from query decomposition avoid this failure. However, query access is not inherently advantageous: strong query-agnostic coverage methods remain competitive or superior in the full-field comparison. Relative to a redundancy-only baseline, structured selection helps most on evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; on broad tasks, the holistic selector improves over either relevance or redundancy alone. Further, pruning reduces cost and memory. These results support a practical design rule: preserve visual coverage by default, and add structured relevance when the task and token budget demand selective evidence retrieval.

items.title: VidToC: Rethinking Video Token Compression for Multimodal Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25574v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.

items.title: EgoWitness: Benchmarking Instance-Level Spatial Memory and Reasoning in Egocentric Video Streams
items.content: arXiv:2611.25849v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.

items.title: Learning Reconstruction Errors as Spatiotemporal Evidence for AI-Generated Video Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.26116v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The proliferation of AI-generated videos has raised growing concerns about misinformation, fraud, and potential societal risks, creating an urgent need for detection. Reconstruction-error-based methods have shown strong empirical performance for AI-generated image detection by exploiting discrepancies between an input and its reconstructed version. Their extension to video detection, however, faces two challenges: (i) a fixed reconstructor is not optimized for the detection objective and may yield weak discriminative signals; and (ii) an additional raw-video feature stream is often introduced to model temporal dependencies, increasing architectural overhead. To address these challenges, we develop a detector that learns and exploits reconstruction errors as a unified source of spatiotemporal evidence. First, we jointly optimize a reconstructor and the downstream classifier to produce reconstruction errors that are more informative for detecting AI-generated videos. Second, we show that consecutive reconstruction errors alone carry temporal evidence, and thus a 3D convolution over them captures spatiotemporal evidence without a raw-video stream. Extensive experiments on over 30 existing AI-video generators demonstrate competitive performance against baselines.

items.reasoning: Addresses a timely and societally important problem (synthetic video detection) with a clear architectural contribution, though it is an incremental extension of an established image-detection paradigm.
