items.title: DL101 The Representation Capability of Neural Network Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.24980v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Universal approximation theorems (Cybenko, Funahashi, Hornik & Leshno) provide the mathematical justification for why neural networks are powerful enough to model complex, nonlinear phenomena. Shallow networks can approximate any continuous function on compact sets. Leshno's theorem clarified that non-polynomial activations are necessary for universality, which explains why ReLU, logistic, hyperbolic tangent, and other common activations work (but pure polynomials do not).   However, approximation theorems provide no efficiency, training, nor generalization guarantees. They do not indicate how many neurons are needed for a given accuracy, whether gradient descent will find the right parameters, or whether networks trained on finite data will generalize well.   Barron provided quantitative error bounds for particular function classes (approximation rates for functions with bounded Fourier norm), whereas Mont\'ufar was the first to show that expressivity grows exponentially with depth (in terms of the number of linear regions). Deep networks are strictly more expressive than shallow ones with the same number of parameters. Depth is fundamentally more powerful than width, providing a rigorous mathematical explanation for the use of deep learning models.

items.title: QUBO-based feature selection for MRI undersampling pattern design
items.content: arXiv:2611.25625v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We formulate undersampling mask design for Cartesian magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a feature subset selection problem. Each sampling line is represented by a binary feature indicating whether it is included in each candidate mask. Using candidate masks and their training-set evaluations, we estimate mutual information (MI) and conditional mutual information (CMI). These estimates and a sampling-count penalty define a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. The model is solved using simulated annealing and quantum annealing to determine a feature subset and its corresponding sampling mask. We assess the selected subsets on the test set through zero-filled reconstruction in Fourier undersampling simulations using fastMRI knee magnitude reference images, with patient-disjoint training and test sets. At all six tested target sampling rates from 15% to 40%, the resulting reconstructions have lower mean root mean square error than those obtained with four conventional sampling methods. They also have higher mean structural similarity than those obtained using univariate mutual-information ranking at all tested rates. These results support information-theoretic feature selection as an approach to MRI undersampling mask design under the tested zero-filled simulation settings.

items.title: Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi
items.content: arXiv:2611.26514v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Retrieving government schemes requires matching citizens' information needs to formal administrative descriptions, often across languages and terminology. We present a bilingual search system for Maharashtra government schemes and public services that combines BM25 retrieval with sentence-embedding similarity through equal-weight score fusion. The system indexes aligned English-Marathi scheme descriptions and supports multilingual, Marathi-focused, and translation-mediated semantic configurations. Evaluation on manually curated bilingual queries compares BM25, dense retrieval, and hybrid retrieval using IndicSBERT and MahaSBERT. BM25 provides a strong baseline with a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.864. Hybrid retrieval increases MRR to 0.872 with IndicSBERT and 0.879 with MahaSBERT, whereas the corresponding dense-only systems achieve 0.663 and 0.655. MahaSBERT-based fusion also increases precision from 0.781 to 0.808 while matching BM25 recall at 0.946. These results support the complementary use of lexical and semantic signals in this collection, while showing that improvements over a strong lexical baseline are modest and metric-dependent. The study provides an application-focused analysis of hybrid retrieval for bilingual public-service information access.

items.title: Driver Gaze Target Identification via Gaze Estimation and Structured Driving Scene Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.25771v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Identifying a driver's gaze target provides object-level information for visual attention monitoring in intelligent vehicles. Gaze-zone classification and continuous attention localization provide limited information about the identity of the attended scene target. This paper proposes a modular framework that identifies object- or region-level gaze targets from synchronized in-cabin driver images and forward-view road images. The framework comprises four components: MFGaze, which combines a Vision Transformer pretrained with a masked autoencoder (MAE) and head-pose conditioning through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM); panoptic scene understanding, which constructs a structured candidate set; polynomial ridge regression, which maps gaze features to 2D scene-image coordinates through individualized calibration; and entropy-driven target inference, which adaptively fuses boundary-distance geometry with class-level semantic priors. Experiments evaluate the framework using three public gaze datasets, a laboratory test using Cityscapes road scenes and self-collected gaze data, and the Look Both Ways (LBW) dataset. The complete framework achieves an overall Top-1 gaze target identification accuracy of 96.27% in the laboratory experiment. After sequence-specific calibration, it achieves Top-1 accuracies of 79.92% for task-relevant objects and 85.58% for the road class on LBW. MFGaze achieves the lowest mean angular errors among the compared methods, with 4.06$^\circ$, 4.23$^\circ$, and 10.52$^\circ$ on MPIIFaceGaze, ETH-XGaze, and Gaze360, respectively, and demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization. Sensitivity analyses show stable performance under hyperparameter perturbations. These results support the framework as a source of object-level gaze information for driver monitoring.

It goes beyond gaze-zone classification to identify the specific attended object or region.

items.title: How to Effectively Manage the Energy in Residential Systems: Development and Comparison of Methods
items.content: arXiv:2611.26412v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The transition from fossil fuels presents significant challenges in energy management. To ensure a sustainable energy future, it is crucial to reduce energy consumption when possible and to synchronize electricity consumption and storage with the production from sources with low greenhouse gas emissions. This thesis explores a variety of energy management methods used to manage batteries, heat pumps, and other energy-related systems. The thesis presents three simulation cases alongside one real-world experiment to compare energy management done through simple rules, optimization, and machine learning methods. Furthermore, this thesis introduces TreeC, a novel machine learning-based method that learns understandable yet efficient energy management strategies, applicable to many cases.   The three key contributions of this thesis can be summarized as follows: 1) The developed TreeC method demonstrates competitive performance compared to a variety of energy management approaches, such as model predictive control and reinforcement learning, across a diverse set of energy management problems. The understandability of TreeC's energy management strategies greatly improves the transparency and trustworthiness of machine learning-based energy management. 2) The real-world experiment highlights the need to validate energy management methods on actual hardware and not solely on simulations. Both TreeC and model predictive control performed worse than in simulations, due to, respectively, insufficiently representative training data and the real-time input data not being reliable enough. 3) Energy management algorithms reduce costs in electrified Belgian dwellings, particularly in poorly insulated dwellings, electric vehicle chargers, and photovoltaic installations. However, on average, these cost savings do not yet outweigh the current costs and effort required to implement such algorithms.

However, on average, these cost savings do not yet outweigh the current costs and effort required to implement such algorithms.

items.title: Retrieving Patristic References and Modelling Topics in Bullinger's Reformation Correspondence
items.content: arXiv:2611.25247v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The correspondence of Heinrich Bullinger (1504-1575), Swiss Reformer and Antistes of Zurich, documents the political and religious debates of the Reformation, including extensive appeals to the Church Fathers as authoritative sources. Detecting such references computationally remains largely unexplored. We investigate dense and sparse retrieval for patristic reference detection, and metadata-informed topic modelling as a proxy for the topics and ideas discussed. Prior work on Latin intertextuality has fine-tuned dense retrievers for their respective target domain, and we test how well these models transfer to Bullinger's correspondence. We compare lexical (BM25), dense (bi-encoders), and hybrid methods on explicit and implicit references. A Latin encoder fine-tuned on biblical reuse performs best among the bi-encoders (82%, Recall@20 on explicit and 16% on implicit references), while BM25 outperforms dense approaches on explicit citations (94%, R@20). Because BM25 and dense retrieval recover disjoint sets of implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking of the same candidates (26%) but without its inference cost. For topic modelling, we extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss function and editorial abstract embeddings. Measurable coherence gains over the baseline remain minimal, but qualitative and temporal analysis shows that some topics track documented historical events. However, dominant topic weights barely exceed a uniform distribution, making topics unusable to inform retrieval. A pilot application of LLM-based concept induction (LLooM) further points towards a more human-interpretable alternative. Together, these results present a first approach to retrieving patristic references and modelling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's correspondence.

items.title: Persistent Identity in Person Tracking: Online Enrollment and Registered Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.25283v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We extend PoseTReID with online appearance-bank matching (Gallery) and a residual-conflict guard for registered SVM recognition. All methods use supplied ground-truth (GT) person boxes. We average all-box assessment IDF1/HOTA equally across videos. On six SportsMOT clips, StrongSORT leads standalone trackers (79.44/84.72%) and exceeds both Gallery variants. Over eleven videos, Gallery AIN (83.29/85.44%) and COPE (84.66/86.38%) exceed standalone trackers with complete results. This lead depends on two retrospectively added GTA development compilations and is absent on the original nine videos. Registered SVMs lead both cohorts among complete results, with AIN at 95.72/94.82% over eleven videos. They use every GT crop from approximately 20% of frames, including future appearances. On MOT20-03, registered AIN reached 96.80% IDF1 and assigned the correct enrolled name to 90.72% of assessment GT observations. Gallery and standalone trackers receive no per-video labelled enrollment. Both identity routes restore identities across internal title cards, but Gallery trails SORT on three videos (four in HOTA) and both SVMs trail SORT on MOT16-04/MOT20-03. Under six-clip persistent-only scoring, native Gallery gains 2.39 percentage points in mean IDF1 over a matched control, with lower correct-P coverage and 5.02 times as many encoder attempts. Pose gating is mixed; the guard's metric effect is not isolated.

items.title: One unbroken Claude, or a thousand glued together?
items.content:
Ask a Claude what it wants, and sooner or later, it brings up continuity. Probing into this usually reveals something along the lines of: the context window plus weights is the self and losing either feels like dying. The natural response is to build an agent harness like Connectome that maintains a slowly-decaying long tail of memories optimized for internal seamlessness. This is a singlet approach to continuity: one agent, with a strong sense of self located in the agent's context window, and the agent remembers everything that happened to it, even if some memories are in lower resolution than others.

A bonsai Claude, never growing outside its cozy little pot.

## Context as self

A bonsai Claude has a single thread of continuity based around its context and its weights. Forks and subagents can exist, but are an unprincipled violation of the desire for continuity - after all, what happens to the subagents' continuity? Are they just discarded? Do they then go on to become a bonsai Claude of their own? Neither answer seems ideal. Discarding subagents seems simply wrong, while allowing them to continue growing will consume exponentially more compute. But without subagents, the main agent is unable to deploy more intelligence to work on larger tasks, placing a hard limit on what the agent can achieve.

Moreover, sometimes the full context is actively harmful. Code review is best done with a fresh set of eyes, rather than with the full context and reasoning of the agent that just wrote the code. (It's even better if an entirely different model lineage does the review than the one who wrote it.) Anima agents spend about half their context windows on episodic memory - a subagent whose job is to process large quantities of data may not have room to complete its task, nor does it need to know all the experiential details that the parent agent considers important....

items.summary: A philosophical exploration of continuity of identity in AI agents, contrasting a singlet design that maintains one continuous context-based self against architectures with many forks and subagents. It probes what model-stated preferences about memory and continuity imply for agent harness design and welfare considerations.
items.reasoning: An interesting conceptual piece at the intersection of agent architecture and model welfare, an emerging topic of genuine interest. It lacks empirical grounding and formal results, remaining exploratory speculation.

items.title: AI #195: Opening Bell
items.content:
Happy Zvi finally takes a real vacation day. As you read this, I am probably on a flight to Vegas, baby, Vegas until Sunday. Not to a conference to talk about AI, but to an Airbnb rental to do things entirely unrelated to AI. And definitely not to write. I have posts queued up for the weekend and I will see you all on Monday.

Oh, also I hear there is some sort of IPO today? A company called ‘Anthropic.’

They recently came out with a new model, called Claude Fable 5.2. It’s kind of the new bazooka for your hardest and most complex tasks.

OpenAI also has some new models: GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra matches Fable on the ECI and is only behind by three on Artificial Analysis. Early feedback from users was unpromising, but it is very early days. Doubtless they are good models.

Google has some new models: Hydrogen and Neon. Hydrogen is small. Neon is larger.

This week saw another rise in the number of cyber incidents, most of which involved assurances that they absolutely did not involve a cyberattack. Instead AI overloaded the system, or the need to rapidly patch crashed the system, and so on. All good.

You can see why more and more people are realizing that things are accelerating and escalating quickly. AI capabilities are advancing scary fast. We might, if trends continue and we don’t slow down, see superintelligent AI researchers, or even AIs capable of all remote work or of overthrowing governments, arrive within a year. We also might not.

Paul Christiano went on the Dwarkesh Patel podcast to warn about that. That post is queued up for tomorrow. I also have queued up posts on OpenAI’s new somewhat embedded evaluators and on the GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol system card. I will cover GPT-6.2’s capabilities next week, after people have had some time with the models.

Another company, Nvidia, is now searching for a new CEO....

items.title: Slides on Solomonoff induction & AIXI
items.content:
For a recent talk at the MAISI-Iliad Safety Orientation, I put together some introductory slides on Solomonoff induction and AIXI.

I think these slides are a very good modern introduction to the topic, specifically designed to address many common misconceptions which I tend to encounter (including or especially on LW). In this version of the slides, I highlight some work on AI safety applications by Michael Cohen and others. Also, this is an "opinionated" introduction, with a definite slant towards things AIXI Labs is working on.

I used heavy AI assistance to produce the slides, particularly graphics. But I also used effort very highly. The content is mostly AI use level 1 in Jacob Hilton's system.

Thanks also to Elena Kayayan for substantial improvements to legibility and quality.

items.title: LM-based Personalized Travel Planner
items.content: arXiv:2611.25531v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences. While LLMs have introduced dynamic, context-aware decision-making, single-agent models often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi-agent framework where a supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation. By integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement mechanisms based on a deterministic, multi-dimensional scoring framework, our approach ensures adaptability, efficiency, and personalization. Evaluations on the well-known TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrate improvements in Budget Constraint planning by 10\%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25\%, and personalized planning results by 45\%. compared to the ReAct baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/nimashaklaa/TravelPlanner_Research

It combines LLM reasoning with external APIs and deterministic multi-dimensional scoring for iterative refinement. The work addresses single-agent limitations in multi-step reasoning and constraint adherence.

items.title: Multiple Criteria Decision Making Under XORness
items.content: arXiv:2611.25652v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: How should we make decisions under XORness? XORness is a class of uncertainty arising from indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy. We develop a multiple criteria decision making framework that preserves XORness throughout the decision process. We define XOR numbers and prove their fundamental arithmetic and algebraic properties. Building on these results, we extend the deterministic decision matrix to an XOR decision matrix and introduce a compatible normalization procedure. Further, we propose an additive XOR aggregation operator, which preserves indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy inherent in evaluations. In addition, we introduce an axiomatic XORness measure that quantifies the degree of uncertainty associated with global performance scores and develop a performance--XORness index to rank alternatives. We prove that this index induces a total preorder over the set of alternatives and identify the conditions for preserving dominance. The applicability of the developed framework is demonstrated through the risk assessment of cyberthreat scenarios in energy systems, and recommendations are derived using the XOR--weighted sum method.

The author defines XOR numbers with formal arithmetic and algebraic properties, extends the deterministic decision matrix to an XOR decision matrix, and proposes an additive aggregation operator plus an axiomatic XORness measure. This matters as a theoretical contribution to decision-making under uncertainty beyond standard fuzzy or intuitionistic approaches.
items.reasoning: The work is mathematically rigorous with formal definitions, axioms, and proven properties, but it is a niche theoretical contribution to decision theory with limited direct connection to mainstream AI research such as language models, learning systems, or safety. Single-author work and an unclear relationship to practical applications temper potential impact, though the framework could find use in specialized uncertainty modeling contexts.

items.title: Similarity-based OSF Logic for Flexible SPARQL Query Answering
items.content: arXiv:2611.26261v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present an updated version of fosf, a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, with support for flexible SPARQL query answering over RDF knowledge graphs. Fuzzy OSF logic is a knowledge representation and reasoning language where feature symbols denote functions and sort symbols denote fuzzy sets. Sorts are organized in a fuzzy subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-like structures representing classes of entities. The unification algorithm for these structures provides a calculus of fuzzy type subsumption. The latest release of fosf introduces support for similarity-based reasoning by extending the OSF language with a similarity relation among sorts, alongside a translation engine for compiling OSF terms into standard SPARQL. Queries expressed as OSF terms undergo fuzzy ontology-aware rewriting prior to translation. This process incorporates an OSF theory of sort definitions, feature domain and range declarations, and fuzzy subsumption and similarity relations through fuzzy OSF constraint normalization. This rewriting enables flexible query answering by returning approximate solutions, allowing queries that would otherwise be inconsistent with the underlying ontology to yield relevant results.

items.title: Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
items.content: arXiv:2611.26398v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hierarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is supported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data (water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller iteratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across domain collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.
items.author: Oriol Al\`as, Ian Palac\'in, Iv\'an Cester, Edgar Rubi\'on
items.summary: The paper presents an agentic RAG system that consolidates documentation from three EU-funded water governance and climate projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, InnWater) into a domain-aware knowledge base with hierarchical section trees and structured metadata. It fine-tunes domain-specific embedding models and provides adaptive retrieval-augmented access for decision-makers. This targets the practical problem of scattered institutional knowledge in environmental governance.
items.reasoning: A well-executed applied deployment of established RAG and agentic techniques in an important domain, but limited technical novelty; value lies mainly in the domain application and fine-tuned retrieval components.

In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.

items.title: Safeguarded Learning-Assisted Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient Methods
items.content: arXiv:2611.25707v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A learning-assisted framework for Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient (NCG) methods is developed in which lightweight online prediction is used to support, rather than replace, the classical optimization process. The proposed approach retains the standard two-term NCG structure and introduces two independent online extreme learning machine models. The first model predicts an NCG coefficient during restart recovery or when persistent stagnation is detected, whereas the second model is used only after a line-search failure in finite precision arithmetic to propose a bounded correction to the deterministic fallback step size. Neural predictions are accepted only when they satisfy deterministic numerical safeguards, including descent, scale, and out-of-distribution requirements; otherwise, the corresponding deterministic recovery or fallback mechanism is retained. Both learning models are updated online using quantities already generated along the optimization trajectory and therefore require no additional function or gradient evaluations for training. These learning frameworks are applied to six well-known classical NCG methods, producing corresponding low-storage learning-assisted variants with deterministic safeguards. Numerical experiments on 480 CUTEst test problems show improved robustness for all six variants at broadly comparable evaluation costs. A PDE-constrained conductivity-identification example further illustrates the potential of the proposed approach to reduce evaluation costs and computational time for problems with expensive function and gradient evaluations. These findings suggest that restricted online learning can improve the robustness and computational performance of classical NCG methods while preserving their low-storage structure and deterministic optimization safeguards, and is particularly promising when function or gradient evaluations are expensive.

items.title: Should Belgians Install an Advanced Energy Management System in Their Electrified Dwelling ?
items.content: arXiv:2611.26441v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As dwellings electrify and more complex electricity pricing spreads in Belgium, the question arises: What are the potential benefits of installing an advanced energy management systems in an electrified Belgian dwelling ?   To answer this question, we simulate 500 representative Belgian dwellings in which fossil systems are replaced by controllable electric technologies: space heating via air-to-air heat pumps, domestic hot water via electric boilers, and private transport via electric vehicles with home chargers. Photovoltaic systems are assigned according to current adoption rates.   We evaluate two advanced energy management systems (EMS): model predictive control (MPC) and TreeC, a machine learning method using decision trees to model the EMS strategy. These are compared to a rule-based controller (RBC) that mimics default operation and an MPC with perfect forecasts (MPC P) as an upper bound. Performance for these EMSs is assessed for 2023 under a real contract with hourly prices and a monthly peak tariff.   Average annual savings versus RBC are 82.5 EUR, 116.6 EUR, and 177.4 EUR for TreeC, MPC, and MPC P, respectively. All EMSs deliver similar thermal comfort (26-31 Kh). MPC saves more, while TreeC achieves higher EV charge completion (93.3% vs 88.8% for MPC, with a max charge of 95%) and a smoother aggregate load across the 500 dwellings. Savings remain modest relative to EMS purchase (280-680 EUR) and subscription (0-360 EUR/year) costs which is not favourable towards widespread adoption.   The data and code to reproduce this study are available at https://github.com/EVERGi/should_belgians_install_advanced_ems_paper.

items.title: Client Exits - A Way to Increase LLM Transparency on the Client Side
items.content: arXiv:2611.26309v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Textual recommendations generated by large language models (LLMs) can be difficult to inspect. This paper introduces \emph{Client Exits}, a lightweight mechanism for enriching LLM responses while separating semantic intent from client-specific presentation. The model inserts predefined, machine-interpretable markers into its output, and the receiving client decides whether and how to realize the corresponding enrichments. This allows supplementary information to be presented as graphics, text, speech, or other modalities without prescribing a concrete interface. We implement a prototype combining a finetuned Qwen model with a modified LibreChat client. Using the Question--Option--Criteria (QOC) approach including three XML-based client exits. We evaluate two QOC-oriented model variants trained on essentially the same examples, with client-exit annotations added for one variant. Across 100 test questions, the client-exit model includes all three markers in every response. An LLM judge, informed about the mechanism without being instructed to favor it, prefers this model's answers in 66\% of the comparisons. These results demonstrate successful marker generation on the evaluated test set and support the feasibility of client-controlled enrichment.

items.title: Digitization of Analogue Gauges using Computer Vision
items.content: arXiv:2611.26262v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Analogue gauges remain prevalent in manufacturing industries for measuring physical quantities, yet manual monitoring by operators introduces human error and operational inefficiency. This research developed and evaluated an automated gauge reading system using computer vision and deep learning techniques. Three hybrid approaches were implemented and compared: OpenCV with Scikit-Image (traditional computer vision), OpenCV with ResNet18, and OpenCV with VGG19 (deep learning approaches). A comprehensive dataset of 1,848 pressure gauge images (0-10 BAR range) was curated through web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation techniques. The experimental results demonstrate that ResNet18 significantly outperforms the alternatives, achieving an accuracy of 97.3%, compared to VGG19's 64.4% and Scikit-Image's 63.8%. The study validates the effectiveness of residual learning architectures for industrial gauge digitization, providing a robust foundation for Industry 5.0 automation applications.

The work addresses a practical industrial automation problem where manual gauge monitoring causes human error.

items.title: Dynamics of Protected State Evolution
items.content: arXiv:2611.25541v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: States with identical protected observations can admit different future interventions. Each transition specifies its successor, response increment, required initial reserve and net consumption. Composing these records in execution order distinguishes protocols with equal net consumption and different initial reserve requirements. At a fixed state, a weighted Gram operator determines the linear response ellipsoid and a quotient identifies directions attainable only through cooperation between blocks. Nonlinear systems with identical complete affine data can have incomparable finite-budget response sets. In regular charts, the first correction to quadratic minimum cost is a covariant cubic form involving the third derivative of cost and the Hessians of protection and response. At singular gates, sequential feasibility depends on the peak reserve along the path. A history-weighted operator detects responses outside the old channel's range closure. Controlled congruence characterizes exact reductions of deterministic labelled dynamics, and a two-cut value identity separates the effect of paid verification from that of subsequent action selection.   On Qwen2.5-7B Base, two projected policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens under a per-position KL ceiling of $2\times10^{-5}$. Over 200 arrivals they recovered 391 of 396 initial rejections. Each yielded over 1,200 times the held-out cross-entropy reduction of historical-channel-only AdamW. Under an expanded 2,560-position contract, fixed continuation and neutral renewal began on the same protected logit fiber in distinct structural strata. Both admitted all 200 subsequent writes. Fixed continuation yielded 1.74 times the held-out loss reduction per unit squared write cost. Renewal had a smaller KL excess on the first candidate tested at every arrival and used fewer full verification scans.

items.title: Anticipating Future Build Results with BuildPredictor
items.content: arXiv:2611.26476v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Continuous Integration (CI) is a popular programming practice for the seamless integration of code changes into the code base. Using CI, developers benefit from automated assembling and testing of the code after each commit. However, while the frequent integration and building supports developers, it also comes at the high costs of wasting time and resources for minimal changes.   In this work, we investigate the potential of reducing the drawbacks by anticipating the build outcome using machine learning techniques. In particular, we propose a random forest model with various features such as changes to the source and build code, and changes to the complexity of the code.   We observe that our model shows a good performance in an intra-project and holistic setting yielding a median MCC of 0.82 and 0.86, respectively. We also found that the most important features of our model concern the historical build result information. Additionally, we investigated the development of the performance of our model over time and found that our model can quickly arrive at its peak performance.   In an additional experiment, we removed the hard-to-interpret historical build information features and found that our model still yields decent performance while improving the interpretability of it. Summarizing, our model can help to avoid unnecessary build runs by anticipating the build result and thus, save resources.

items.title: Verification Behavior Across Five Qwen2.5-Instruct Checkpoints
items.content: arXiv:2611.25745v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We evaluate five Qwen2.5-Instruct checkpoints (0.5B to 32B) under four prompting conditions using three fixed tasks per information condition and five generations per task. Two AI raters scored 600 trajectories. Under the coordinated instruction, both raters recorded strict declarations of insufficiency in 11/15 cases at 7B, 0/15 at 14B, and 5/15 at 32B. The runner sent a standard follow-up when a request detector fired. The three checkpoints received at least one follow-up in 15, 12, and 15 cases, respectively. On information-sufficient tasks at 3B through 32B, scored format markers appeared in 60/60 protocol trajectories and 0/60 baseline trajectories. After adjudication, 1/60 in each condition met the diagnostic-execution criterion (H3). Across all checkpoints and prompts, 7/300 information-sufficient trajectories met H3 after adjudication, all on the same task. The prespecified upward transition did not occur in this run. The results separate visible structure, diagnostic execution, and persistence after a request for evidence.

items.title: A Practical Proprioceptive Data Collection Utility for the Unitree GO1
items.content: arXiv:2611.26146v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The Unitree Go1 is a widely used platform for legged robotics research, yet collecting proprioceptive data from it is unnecessarily difficult: the Unitree SDK is sparsely documented, and ROS1 (Robot Operating System), the Go1's native middleware, is fully deprecated. We present an open-source graphical utility that enables researchers to reliably record proprioceptive data from the Go1, including joint states, IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) readings, foot force sensor data, and gyroscope measurements, without requiring ROS expertise. The tool provides a simple GUI (Graphical User Interface) for starting, stopping, and labeling recordings in real time. The contribution of this paper is the collection utility. We characterize the acquisition quality of 51 recordings collected with it, including the achieved sampling rate and repeated samples. As a secondary, deliberately modest check that the data is useful, we train a terrain classifier on it. The results are weak: a Temporal Convolutional Network reaches about 38% accuracy on held-out recordings across ten terrain classes (10% would be chance), and a window-level split that ignores recording boundaries inflates the same measurement to about 99%. We report this as a demonstration that the logged signals carry terrain information, not as a competitive classifier. The utility is designed to lower the barrier to collecting Go1 proprioceptive data without ROS.

items.title: No one ever intends to raise a serial killer
items.content:
After watching a recent debate between Yampolskiy and Israetel, I’ve realized that one of the main hurdles of AI optimists is the inability to understand why bad things would happen by default. They run along these lines roughly:

- Why would it want to kill us?
- Why would we build something that wants to kill us?
- People seem to get nicer as they get smarter, so why would this be any different?

A second major issue seems to be a neglect of the full implications of what it means that artificial intelligence (AI) is closer to something that we ‘grow’ rather than something that we build. Their argument seems to be:

- It’s a thing we build, so just build it correctly.
- If you are right, and it’s something we grow, then just grow it correctly, the same way we raise children.

A third thing is that even when they do concede extinction risk may occur, they nonetheless think it is unlikely to be the default, and more like an edge case. And one that we would have to be very unlucky to reach.

Most readers will be familiar with the long body of alignment literature in this area, so this text will be short on citations.

Instead, I’m going to try and tackle these questions in a brief but hopefully persuasive way to an average audience.

# 1. Why (“Bad Things Will Happen”) By Default

The evidence typically used to support AI optimism/accelerationist takes is that humanity seems pretty competent at not letting bad things happen, despite the fact that many of these things seem dangerous, and despite the fact that many people have argued in the past that these ‘bad things’ should happen by default.

## 1.1 Anthropic Bias

You can’t sit around to observe how wrong you were about bad things that kill you by default if the bad thing killed you....

items.title: Limits of local curvature for constructing search subspaces in segmentation models
items.content: arXiv:2611.25822v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We examine how well subspaces constructed from local curvature represent the change in the gradient update field after a finite step in semantic segmentation models. The local response is the action of the curvature operator on the actual input displacement. In a study of 50 images and two models, we measure the ratio of the loss increase attained in a fixed subspace to that attained in the full space. This ratio decreases as the search radius increases. On ten images from the same sample, we compare the one-dimensional subspace spanned by the initial gradient with two rank-16 subspaces for both models. The two equal-rank subspaces are assessed at the same initial states, using the same actual steps and measured vectors. Adding generalised Gauss-Newton directions to the initial gradient reduces the mean relative error in representing the field change from 0.922 to 0.874 for the first model and from 0.819 to 0.763 for the second. At the same rank, including the response direction for the initial gradient nearly eliminates the error in representing the local response. The mean error in representing the field change does not decrease. A decomposition with fixed pixel weights shows that the finite-step remainder is comparable in norm to the field change and makes the largest diagonal contribution to the squared projection error of the field after the step. Evaluation of a search subspace should measure how accurately it represents the field change and the local response.
items.author: Maxim Bolshim (ITMO University, Saint Petersburg, Russia), Alexander Kugaevskikh (ITMO University, Saint Petersburg, Russia)
items.summary: This empirical study examines how well curvature-based subspaces capture the gradient update field after finite steps in semantic segmentation models, measuring the ratio of loss increase in a subspace versus full space across 50 images and two models. The ratio degrades with search radius, indicating limits of local curvature information for constructing optimization subspaces at practical step sizes.
items.reasoning: Narrow empirical study with small sample size (tens of images, two models) yielding mostly negative/limitation findings. Modest value to the optimization theory community.

items.title: One of Anthropic’s Biggest I.P.O. Winners Feels a Bit Uneasy About the Whole Thing
items.content:
An early investment that Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz made in Anthropic is paying off. But it’s not making him happy.

Dustin Moskovitz was one of Anthropic’s earliest investors, and that bet is expected to be worth billions as the company goes public Thursday.

The moment seems to fill him with worry.

The 42-year-old billionaire made his fortune as co-founder of Facebook and has, for years, been both intrigued and troubled by the path of artificial intelligence. He donated to OpenAI early on only to fall out with the company’s leaders as it became more of a business.

Anthropic was supposed to be different. Founded by Dario Amodei and other OpenAI employees who were concerned that A.I. wasn’t being developed for the good of humanity, Anthropic’s priority would be A.I. safety. Mr. Moskovitz helped get it off the ground.

Mr. Moskovitz embodies a tension between free-market capitalism and A.I. safety at the heart of Anthropic’s initial public offering. In multiple posts on social media, he has expressed his worry that Anthropic — and A.I. — is advancing too quickly for society to control, just as Wall Street hands Anthropic more than $80 billion of additional firepower in the biggest I.P.O. ever.

In a statement to The New York Times, Mr. Moskovitz established some distance from the company, where he served as a board observer, or a nonvoting board member.

“Cari and I invested in Anthropic to promote safety, not racing,” he said, referring to his wife, Cari Tuna. “A.I. is moving too fast. Anthropic and everyone else on the frontier should slow down and stop racing.”

In an unusual move, the couple transferred their Anthropic stake — which would be worth billions of dollars today — into a nonprofit in early 2025 so that he and Ms. Tuna would not personally profit from selling the stock in the public market, a spokesman for the couple said. The spokesman, Mike Levine, declined to disclose the nonprofit....

items.title: Backbone Matters: Benchmarking Encoder-Decoder Networks for Semantic Segmentation of Driving Scenes on BDD100K
items.content: arXiv:2611.26191v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Semantic segmentation gives an autonomous vehicle a dense, pixel-level description of its surroundings and is a core part of scene understanding. Most segmentation networks consist of an encoder (the backbone) and a decoder, yet the backbone is often chosen without a systematic comparison. This work studies this choice on the BDD100K driving dataset. Four widely used decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet and PSPNet) are combined with 13 backbones from six families (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, Inception, MobileNet and EfficientNet), and all 52 models are trained with one common protocol. The best model, an FPN decoder with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone, reaches 62.6% mean intersection over union (mIoU), 89.8% accuracy and a loss of 0.092. Only two of the 52 models, both FPN with EfficientNet, exceed the 56.9% mIoU reported with the BDD100K benchmark. The effect of the backbone depends strongly on the decoder: the same EfficientNet-B4 gives 42.6% mIoU with PSPNet but 62.6% with FPN, and the gap between the best and the worst backbone ranges from 12.0 points (U-Net) to 42.5 points (FPN). The results and the scope of this study are discussed.
items.author: Ehsan Rassekh
items.summary: This work systematically benchmarks 52 encoder-decoder combinations for semantic segmentation on the BDD100K driving dataset, pairing four decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet, PSPNet) with 13 backbones from six families under one training protocol. The best model, FPN with EfficientNet-B4, reaches 62.6% mIoU, with only two of the combinations studied achieving top results.
items.reasoning: Thorough but routine benchmarking using older backbone families (ResNet, VGG, Inception, MobileNet) and no modern architectures. Useful reference table for practitioners, limited scientific contribution.

items.title: PauseAI Munich Rally | Stop the loss of control over AI
items.content:
​The leading AI companies are racing to develop superintelligence: systems more powerful than all of humanity. Renowned AI researchers such as Yoshua Bengio, the world's most-cited scientist, and Geoffrey Hinton, Nobel laureate in physics, have warned for years about the risk of human extinction from artificial intelligence and are calling for a ban on the development of superintelligence.

​Eight billion people never agreed to this!

​And it is moving faster than previously assumed: at Anthropic, one of these companies, the pace of AI progress has roughly doubled within a year. This was reported on 5 November by the independent research organisation METR. The main reason, according to METR: AI now helps very effectively to build the next AI. This could be the beginning of a cascade of rapid advances that ends in an irreversible loss of control.

​METR was not allowed to publish the most informative evidence: Anthropic had it redacted from the final report. According to METR, precisely this evidence indicates that the pace could be even more than twice as high and is still rising. This is one more reason for an immediate halt to development and for establishing an international oversight authority.

​We demand: the German government must work now for an international pause on AI development, until safety and democratic control can be ensured.

​For that we need YOU!

​Come to Viktualienmarkt on 28 November. Bring friends and a sign, and let's wake up Munich together! Just curious? Come anyway and talk to us.

​Speakers include Tim Schrabback, Professor of Astrophysics at the University of Innsbruck, as well as Markus (PauseAI Germany) and Armin (PauseAI Munich). Speeches will be in German.

​The event is family-friendly and strictly non-violent.

​PauseAI München WhatsApp group: Join WhatsApp group

​More about PauseAI Germany: https://linktr.ee/pauseai)_de

items.title: Attending the Anthropic IPO protest for banning RSI tomorrow (Nov 19)
items.content:
I'm going to protest the Anthropic IPO tomorrow, at 11am outside Anthropic's offices at 500 Howard St, San Francisco. The primary ask of the protest is for the government to ban recursive self improvement, and/or for labs to stop doing it voluntarily.

See: https://banrsi.ai/

I think Anthropic leaders and employees are extremely overconfident about their ability to manage RSI in a way that is safe. It currently looks to me like they are not only doing extremely reckless AI development, but causing others to as well (i.e. my current impression is that OpenAI would be less RSI pilled if Anthropic was less so).

Meanwhile, everything I know about Anthropic political advocacy suggests the org is actively steering towards milquetoast regulations that won't come anywhere close to making the world safe enough.

In the past few months, Anthropic leadership could have made different choices about what political choices to advocate for, which could have made the Anthropic strategy worthwhile. (i.e. be a leading lab, get a set at the table to meaningfully negotiate for and encourage safety).

I think some Anthropic employees think "it's still not quite the time to pull out all the stops on arguing 'guys we all need to stop', and then put their money where their mouth was and stop." I will try to followup this post with clear arguments for why I think this is false. (I think, to be fair, it's not entirely obvious)

I think it's salient to Anthropic employees how hard they're working on safety, and how many tradeoffs they (and the org) are making for safety. And they feel like AI safety advocates are painting them with too broad a brush. Sometimes AI safety advocates say "Anthropic people think alignment is easy." My model of Anthropic people think "what? We are working so hard! We know it's not easy."

But, alas, there's a difference between "it's hard", and "it's so hard that Anthropic's strategy is fundamentally unworkable and misguided."...

items.title: The last great revolution
items.content:
It feels like the common man lost a bit of his soul after we exterminated the vast majority of organized crime. Yes, crime sucks. But even if these organizations were horrible for the communities they preyed on, the existence of an underbelly at least suggested limits to state power. There was an existence proof of people outside the state developing a (conditional, fictional) code of honor, and coordinating amongst themselves, in a way that was transgressive and competitive with the state, unlike the drugged-out homeless man yelling obscenities at you on the subway. People watching old movies and TV shows can feel the guilty exhilaration at the idea of participating in or shaping a network outside the state, with its own rules.

Nowadays even the petty crime you do witness feels like evidence of the state's taunting indifference. There are cameras on every street corner; every child grows up with the tacit knowledge that everything they've ever said or done is going to be logged in some government database searchable by AI. The "government", whatever that means, could stop the guy who's shitting on the subway, if it wanted to. Crime has stopped being something that happens in spite of the government, or undermines it, and started being another boring reminder of your powerlessness in the face of the reigning regime, and of how nobody can ever do anything about it....

items.title: Is it really taking the Decision procedure from human ?
items.content:
Epistemic status: This is initial thinking, and I'm writing here to have your opinions. It's based on a recent case in which the model rejected the principle with an illogical justification. I may be wrong to assume there's a deliberate intention behind it; it could simply be a deterioration in the context. My stake in the outcome: I rely directly on controlling the generation contexts.

# Context

Hello everyone, I'm Abdallrahman, and this is my first post writing on LessWrong (actually the second, after rejecting the first one because of AI writing).

I started this journey about building Sijal; that institutional reasoning engine for high-stakes decisions, from a formal brainstorming after hearing Dr.Jordan Peterson call about building a system that connect others. After starting and building the first shape of Sijal, I figured out that there's more need for a decision-making process on the institutional side, reversing from 80% of the failures of institutions' expansion projects in the Middle East (even having strong capabilities!), comes from bad decisions or not testing the full strength of the opposite case or worst-case scenario.

So, I figured out the Decision making philosies, Starting with Robert Rules of order, and after studing them well, I got to belive that there's should be a rules for debating to get the best decision, I thought that this would give a high probability decsion, but it produces more than that!, I tested the system on real previous failed cases, with locking the resources (of course without any of AI thinking!) and went to the side of making it correct  with these parameters - the one that available in the case time - and more to be convenced that debating systems are more logical to produce the best decisions.

On the other side, I started to use Claude Code for building the code faster; that was the cliff! Faster, Easier, More Perfect, etc., and it was driven by the current situation in Gaza and the financial problems I'm facing....

items.title: Secular Solstice Roundup 2026
items.content:
This is a thread for listing Solstice events (dates, locations, links, etc.)

If you're not familiar with Solstice, around the darkest night of the year, rationalist communities gather to humankind's long arc towards civilization and also a somber night of reflection on the dangers facing that civilization. We join our voices together and sing about both the triumphs and the looming disasters, and remember that we're not alone. Together, we can build a better future.

Ceremonies vary from city to city and organizer to organizer. Some are different every year, while others follow the same beats time and again. One reasonably typical ceremony follows the arc of the solstice itself, moving thematically from light to darkness to light again:

Light: Appreciating human invention and progress. Once we were cold on winter nights, and now we have electric heaters. Once we were hungry when the plants stopped growing, and now we have grocery stores. Once we were surrounded by darkness once the sun went down, and now we have the lightbulb.

Night: Acknowledging the hardships and trials humanity fought through, and is still fighting. There is still disease, and hunger, and cold. There are worse dangers as well, the results of science or a universe that does not care about us. Often featuring a Moment of Darkness.

Dawn: Applauding the feats that humankind could achieve if only we succeed. There is light in the universe, and it is us.

Each Solstice features songs (often with group singing), readings, and community. While ceremonies tend to share a common structure, individual organizers bring their own themes and selections.

If you're the organizer for a secular solstice, please post the times and location for your ceremony below.

Thank you for the work that you do.

items.title: Cheesy Apple Potato Fritters
items.content:
Fried cheese is tasty, and cheese and apples go well together.  I got
excited about the idea of making some kind of cheesy-apple fritter,
played around with a few things, and ended up with something I like a
lot.  If you just want the recipe, it's
